subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) moved:
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the fourth and final report of a special committee on the defence of Canada regulations, presented to the house on the 4th instant, be now concurred in.
He said: Since very little of this report has been brought to the attention of the public it might be appropriate to say a few words by way of explanation.
As hon. members of this house know, the defence of Canada regulations are issued under the authority of the War Measures Act for the protection of the realm and the safety of the state, for the efficient prosecution of the war, and to protect Canada and her people from the activities of the enemy. The responsibility for administration of these regulations rests with the government and has been entrusted to the heads of various departments: the Minister of Justice, the Secretary of State, the Minister of National Defence, and, in some respects, the Minister of Transport. The regulations provide for protection against those who would give themselves to espionage activities or acts likely to assist the enemy.
The reasons for these regulations have been given to the public on many occasions; and of course, being rules passed during war time, in their nature and operation they are restrictive of the general liberties of the subject. Because of that fact, in some quarters they have not been altogether accepted, and in many instances have been criticized. The regulations were passed the day following the declaration of war, and have been in force ever since. During the last session a committee was appointed which studied the regulations and recommended certain amendments which were thought desirable in view of existing circumstances. Again this year,

Defence of Canada Regulations
on March 4, the house appointed a committee to look further into the regulations and report to the house as to what it might be advisable to suggest to His Excellency the Governor General by way of amendment. The committee held twenty-four meetings; a subcommittee was appointed, and the final report of the committee was made on June 4, appearing in Votes and Proceedings of that date.
The principal recommendations contained in that report were made for the purpose of giving the assurance that the administration of such regulations would afford full protection to those who might be affected by them; but before the final report was made an interim report was presented on April 3, containing suggested amendments to rules 26A, 26B and 37A, which amendments were accepted immediately by his excellency and at once implemented. The effect of these amendments was that persons who are nationals of and who were born in Czechoslovakia should be excluded from the categoiy of enemy aliens. The report was concurred in and adopted by the house.
During the course of its deliberations the committee was fortunate in having appear before it Mr. Alexander Patterson, his majesty's commissioner of prisons for Great Britain, who happened to be in Canada in connection with the internees sent to this country from Britain and who gave your committee valuable information as to the manner in which similar regulations were administered in Great Britain.
Your committee has recommended important amendments to regulation 15. If hon. members will refer to the defence of Canada regulations they will find that regulation 15 reads:
The Secretary of State of Canada may make provision by order for preventing or restricting the publication in Canada of matters as to which he is satisfied that the publication, or, as the case may be, the unrestricted publication, thereof would or might be prejudicial to the safety of the state or the efficient prosecution of the war, and an order under this paragraph may contain such incidental and supplementary provisions as may appear to the Secretary of State to be necessary or expedient for the purposes of the order including provisions for securing that documents, pictorial representations, photographs or cinematograph films shall, before publication, be submitted or exhibited to such authority or person as may be specified in such order.
The Secretary of State is entrusted with the duty and obligation of prohibiting the publication of pamphlets or other documentary propaganda which may be subversive, and he 
has the responsibility of declaring that such publications or newspapers are carrying on subversive activities. Some people, however, think this power might be subject to abuse; that it is altogether too much power to be given to one person, and that there is danger that such power might be used-not by the present incumbent of the office, but by possible successors-to restrict the publication of documents which could not be considered subversive. Therefore the committee has considered it advisable to recommend that the Secretary of State be authorized to call in someone to pass upon his orders when those concerned felt justified in appealing from his decision.
If the report of the committee is adopted, the following will be added to regulation 15:
(3)	Any person against whom an order is made under this section may take objection to such order to. a committee appointed by the Minister of Justice to consist of a person who holds or has held high judicial office.
(4)	When objection is taken, the functions of such committee shall be to consider and make recommendations to the Secretary of State with respect to any objections against such order which are duly made to the committee by the person to whom such order relates.
(5)	Notice of objection shall be made to the Secretary of State within fourteen days from the date of service of the order in question, which order shall contain a provision notifying the person of his right to make objection and shall refer to the publication or publications in respect of which the order has been made.
(6)	On receipt of any such notice of objection, the Secretary of State shall forthwith notify such committee who shall make arrangements for the hearing of such objection.
In the event of the adoption of these recommendations the person or persons affected by the suppression of publications would have the right to object to the order of the Secretary of State, such objection to be heard by a person occupying or having occupied high judicial office. His report would be made to the Secretary of State.
A further recommendation of some importance suggests the repeal of regulation 22, and the substitution of another section. Hon. members are no doubt aware that section 21 provides for the detention of persons who are believed to be carrying on subversive activities. This regulation applies to British subjects, and the onus is placed upon the Minister of Justice of dealing with the liberty of such persons. Strong exception has been taken to the procedure which has heretofore been followed in dealing with these persons. Some critics have gone so far as to say that no such person should be arrested, detained or interned, without first having been tried as

Dejence of Canada Regulations
to the justification for such detention. The committee has found that in the past, while there has been no abuse in the administration of these regulations, there might have been some justification in the minds of some people for apprehension as to t'he safety of persons who might have been detained without just cause. The committee recommends therefore slight changes in procedure, so that assurance may be given to the public that those who are detained will have full opportunity of appealing from the detention order made by the Minister of Justice. Under the amendment they may have their cases reviewed, and are given the opportunity to offer evidence in support of their contentions.
Heretofore an appeal from an order of detention was made to a committee of one, and it was stipulated that such person must hold high judicial office. It has been claimed that this provision is not wide enough, and that the tribunal hearing an appeal should consist of more than one person. The committee recommends therefore that it consist of three persons, the chairman being a person holding or having held high judicial office.

Yes, that is correct. The expression "high judicial office" applies only to regulation 15. In regulation 22 the word "high" has been eliminated, and the chairman may now be a person holding judicial office.
Perhaps it would be well if I were to place on record the regulation suggested in substitution for the present regulation 22. The committee recommends:
That regulation 22 be repealed and that the following regulation, to be numbered 22, be substituted therefor:
22. (1) Any person aggrieved by the making of an order against him under the powers conferred by the last preceding regulation may make his objection to an advisory committee as provided in this regulation.
(2)	For the purpose of this regulation the Minister of Justice shall appoint one or more advisory committees, each to consist of three persons, to consider and make recommendations to him with respect to any objections against an order made under the last preceding regulation. The number of committees appointed shall, in the opinion of the Minister of Justice, be adequate to deal promptly with the oases arising in the different parts of Canada.
(3)	The chairman of each committee shall be nominated by the Minister of Justice and shall be a person who holds or has held judicial office.
(4)	As soon as possible after detention under an order made under the provisions of the last preceding regulations, the person agninst whom the order is made shall in every case be informed
of the general grounds on which he is detained and notice of his detention shall, where possible and not contrary to the public interest, be given to his family or such person as he may request.
(5)	It shall be the duty of the Minister of Justice to secure that every person detained as aforesaid is informed of his right to make an objection under this regulation.
(6)	A person desiring to make an objection shall deliver to the person having his custody a written notice of objection, signed by the objector, within thirty days from the date of such detention or such further time as the Minister of Justice in his discretion may allow, and a true copy of such notice shall forthwith be forwarded by the person aforesaid to the Minister of Justice for transmission to the chairman of a committee.
(7)	The chairman on receipt of such notice of objection shall give such directions as may be convenient and necessary for the prompt and just disposition of the objection.
(8)	It shall be the duty of the chairman to inform the objector within a reasonable time before the hearing of the grounds on which the order has been made against him, and, in order to enable him to present his case, to furnish him with as full particulars of the reasons for such order as in the opinion of the chairman the circumstances permit, and such particulars shall be further supplemented by the committee at the hearing by giving the objector all such further particulars as it shall deem necessary and advisable.
(9)	The objector may be represented by counsel, solicitor or agent.
(10)	The hearing may take place at ,any place and it may be adjourned from time to time as the committee shall determine. The Minister of Justice shall cause to be put before the committee all the information about such person available to the minister except such as is not in the public interest to disclose.
(11)	Where the Minister of Justice has referred a recommendation of an advisory committee to the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in order that the latter may have an opportunity of putting such further material as he may desire before the minister, the commissioner shall submit such material within a delay of fifteen days or such further time as the minister may allow.
(12)	The chairman or any member of a committee may administer oaths, and a committee may receive and accept such evidence and information on oath, affidavit or otherwise as m its discretion it may deem fit and proper.
(13)	A committee shall have all the powers and authority of a commissioner appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act, chapter 99 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927.
(14)	The Minister of Justice may make further rules as to the manner in which objections against an order ,as aforesaid may be made and 'disposed of.
(15)	The committee shall consider and make recommendations on any matter arising under these regulations which may be referred to it by the Minister of Justice.
These are the main recommendations made to the house by the committee in connection with regulations 15 and 22.

A minor amendment is suggested to regulation 39, which has to do with the spreading of reports or the making of statements prejudicial to the public interest or the carrying on of the war. A recommendation is made in respect to persons who "aot in a manner prejudicial" to his majesty or who .nterferes with the success of his majesty's forces. A recommendation is made in connection with regulation 58, covering the forfeiture of articles seized by the police and providing that forfeiture and destruction of such articles may be ordered by the Attorney General of Canada or the attorney general of any province.
A recommendation is made that internees be segregated according to their classification. A recommendation is made 'hat internees be given the privilege of receiving visitors provided that it is not against the public interest. The committee also recommends that before a person is taken to a detention camp he should be detained in the gaol or other place of confinement nearest to his place of residence.
It is hoped that these recommendations will be accepted by the house. It is true that in some respects they would seem to change the condition of affairs which has hitherto existed. The committee recommends that the chairman of each committee shall be a person who holds or has held judicial office. It has been brought to our attention that in Great Britain all the members of the committees are laymen and that it might be possible that a superior court judge or a judge of the high court would find it difficult at times to preside permanently.
I move that the report of the committee be adopted.

speechtext: What did the committee find with regard to naturalization and deportation?

The committee did not have much time to go into those matters, but studied them sufficiently to be able to report that it would appear that the naturalization and immigration laws would not need to be amended at the present time, because they are not being used to any considerable extent. Before the war is over, however, it is possible that they may have to be revised.
The committee recommends:
Your committee has received some evidence and has investigated these two important subjects in part only and, notwithstanding the fact that your committee has held a great many meetings, including on occasions two meetings a day. the limited time at our command has made it impossible to devote the time to these subjects which they require in order to enable a proper report to be made to the house.

Your committee therefore respectfully begs to recommend that at the next session of the house the law relating to naturalization and deportation and matters incidental thereto be the subject matter of a reference to a committee of the house.
The committee felt that the law with respect to naturalization will have to be amended, in respect to procedure if not in principle. The same is true with respect to the law having to do with immigration and deportation. In view of changing conditions and the possible influx of immigration after the war, the committee thought it might be well that a committee of the house should be set up at the next session, or later if necessary, to study these two subjects exclusively.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report which has just been presented by the chairman of the special committee on the defence of Canada regulations is the result of a careful and prolonged inquiry extending virtually over two sessions, because many of the members of the committee this year were members of the committee which sat in the previous session. During that time the committee held some fifty meetings, besides numerous sittings of its subcommittee; and incidentally I was a member of both the main committee and the subcommittee.
It appears to me that differences of opinion regarding the regulations and their administration are due to fundamental differences in approach. Some take the view that the regulations and final decisions should be administrative matters. Whilst the majority in both years took that view, a minority was of the opinion that the procedure should more nearly approximate a judicial procedure, and that at least the final decisions ought not to be left to the minister and his advisers. Because what I may call the administrative view prevailed, to that extent I was not able to approve the report.
But the main recommendations in the report do meet with my approval, and if carried out I believe they will do much to remove important objections to the present

Defence of Canada Regulations
procedure. I strongly urge upon the government the adoption of the recommendation affecting regulations 21 and 22.
Since regulation 21 as it originally stood is a serious departure from the normal course of court procedure and traditional British justice, every effort should be made to minimize the dangers to justice inherent in the regulation. This becomes I think more important and necessary since the passage of orders in council such as the one which was announced last Friday, P.C. 4061, bringing the coal mining industry under the regulations.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What
section 'brings them under the regulations?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order in council 4061 brings the coal mining industry under the defence of Canada regulation section 2 (d) by declaring it to be an essential service. It seems to me that an order in council affecting an industry in which organization is going on and has in some respects been established might have been considered in the house when we were discussing labour questions, as we were last week, and should not have been brought before the public simply by order in council. The use of the regulations against men engaged in the organization of even illegal strikes will in my opinion play directly into the hands of some whose real purpose may be to cause internal strife.
I regret that the committee could not adopt the proposal for an inquiry by a committee of three persons before a detention order was actually made. I should say in fairness, however, that evidence furnished to the committee showed that with proper safeguards the powers of preventive detention conferred upon the government under section 21 are necessary for the safety of the state. But unfortunately cases have arisen which indicate that in some instances the powers may not have been wisely used. The detention of Doctor Levine of Toronto, for example, after he had served his gaol sentence, and the arrest of Jaimes A. Murphy whilst engaged in negotiations with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on behalf of a group of its employees, have given rise to suspicion and uneasiness, and at least these two cases should be referred at the earliest possible day, for immediate investigation, to the committee which is recommended under the new section 22. If this is done under the proposed new section, appeals will [DOT]be heard under conditions which will in my opinion ensure a fairer hearing than has hitherto been possible under the practice which has prevailed. Consequently I am strongly in favour of the immediate adoption of regulation 22 as recommended by the committee. Advisory committees of three
persons presided over by a judge, provided that they are sufficiently numerous to deal promptly with objections, are in line with suggestions that we have made in the House of Commons and which have been urged by many organizations all across the country.
The new regulations, it will be noted, also require the chairman of the committee to furnish the accused with as full particulars of the charge as circumstances permit, and further obligate the committee at the hearing to supplement the particulars by giving all such further information as the committee shall deem necessary and advisable. This, it seems to me, is an important step in advance of the regulations as they have stood up to the present time. The accused, as the chairman indicated, may be represented by counsel; the hearing may be adjourned to give further opportunity of the production of evidence, and the minister is obliged to give the committee all information available about the person which it is in the public interest to disclose. I do not like that proviso, for it seems to me that a committee of the type contemplated ought to be as carefully chosen and as trustworthy as the civil servants who have access to all the information and who advise the minister regarding these cases. I do not think that judges and other persons who have the confidence of the minister to a sufficient extent to be appointed to these committees, should be denied any information that may assist them in obtaining a comprehensive and accurate view of the case.
Section 22 is also improved by suggesting that when the minister refers the committee's recommendation to the commissioner of the mounted police he shall submit within a period of fifteen days any further material he desires to submit. I think this should do much to obviate the danger of delay in final decisions, which delays, of course, have been a cause of dissatisfaction and suspicion.
The committee, I am glad to say, also recommended improvements in the procedure under regulation 39, dealing with organizations, publications, and so forth, banned under the regulations by order in council. I wish the words "or likely" to do something were eliminated from the regulations where they appear. In my opinion the interpretation placed upon them in some cases, particularly in the early part of the war, caused suffering and hardship and gave rise to suspicion of the regulations and their purpose generally. Apart from that, the recommendation that publishers of banned publications be given a right of appeal to a committee consisting of a person who has held or holds high judicial office will tend to a better administration of that regulation.
Defence of Canada Regulations

I strongly urge the adoption by the government of section 7 and 8 of the report. It has seemed to me that regulations regarding the writing of letters to their families and receiving visits from them ought not to be the same for interned British subjects as for prisoners of war. Under proper supervision, there should be no difficulty in liberalizing present internment regulations for Canadian citizens.
I am glad in somewhat the same connection to support whole-heartedly the recommendation which was made, and adopted by the house, to remove citizens of Czechoslovakia from the category of enemy aliens. I think that that was a matter of justice which was somewhat delayed.
While, for reasons which I think I have indicated, I did not support the adoption of the report when it was before the committee, I believe that its adoption by the house is a step in the right direction, as a return to more democratic procedure; and I hope that next session a committee will recommend still further modifications towards the restoration of the rule of law. In any event the present report indicates a desire to maintain more of our elementary democratic rights than has been evidenced since the outbreak of war. Tn common with others of the democratic, faith, I believe that we must be vigilant to see that reactionary forces do not succeed in destroying democracy at home whilst we are engaged in a struggle for democracy abroad; and every step towards the suppression of legitimate labour organizations, of the publication of proper comment on the activities of the government, and so on, plays into the hands of those who have the same general fundamental point of view as Hitler and those who support him.
Nor, may I say, on the other hand, must we allow our vigilance for British freedom to be imposed upon and used by subversive elements who pay lip-service to democracy in order to destroy the very basis of freedom in this country. We must guard against the would-be Hitlers and the would-be Stalins in our midst, for in regard to democracy and freedom, their objective is the same-its destruction. The unholy alliance between the forces of nazism and communism must be recognized and opposed. A United States writer coined a neat and, it seems to me, an appropriate name for their activities, which he described as communazism. In that regard, I might add, the economic agreements between Hitler and Stalin make Russia the economic ally of nazi Germany. Thus, Russia now has a stake in a German victory, a fact clearly emphasized by Russia's non-aggression

pact with a ruthless Japanese imperialism murderously invading China and threatening freedom in the far east.
In this country, communists and their sympathizers whisper that the masses of our people would be no worse off under Hitler; and that, of course, is dangerously false and subversive propaganda. Actually, people who believe in political and economic democracy have a tremendous stake in the outcome of this war; for upon it depend our economic progress .and our freedom. Wherever Hitler has gone, people's cooperatives, trades unionism, religious freedom, and all the freedoms have disappeared. Conditions were and are bad in our democratic countries, but they are infinitely better than those in Germany and German-controlled territories, and I hope that our people who are being subjected to the type of propaganda I have just mentioned will bear constantly that fact in mind. Here, men and women of diverse views may organize and agitate to achieve their objectives, but in the communazi totalitarian countries those who oppose the dictators are slaughtered, or imprisoned without any trial or appeal, or are forced to flee for refuge to the democratic countries. The fate of social democrats, trade union leaders, and leaders in the cooperative movement in the countries overrun by Hitler bears tragic witness to this. The very fact that in this house we can discuss, criticize, and try to amend-yes, and succeed in amending-the defence of Canada regulations gives the lie to the communazi propaganda in favour of a peace which would be a Hitler victory.
To say, as some are doing, that this is another imperialist war fought for economic and financial reasons, just another attempt to fasten the Chains of international finance upon the world which ought to be opposed, is of course also a propaganda to undermine our determination to see this thing through. If that were so, we in this group, at least, would be opposing this war as vigorously as we criticized preparations for such a war when powerful interests in our own commonwealth were building up Hitler and Mussolini and seeking an understanding with them.

As to this present war being a war promoted for economic and imperialistic interests in the economic sense of the word "imperialistic", I would say that this is the first time in British history at least that the people of Britain forced a large portion of their government to take a stand in opposition to the interests which they, some members of the government themselves,, favoured.

It is not my function as a member of parliament to act as a special agent for the government. But where I have direct knowledge of sabotage or anything of the kind I shall deem it my duty to inform the government.
The stirring up of discontent at this time could not be successful unless conditions were present which make for its success. So that in carrying out these regulations the government should endeavour to distinguish at all times between legitimate discontent with regard to bad conditions and the promotion of discontent for ulterior motives. That is why we have always contended that there should be a complete and fair hearing for every person accused under the defence of Canada regulations. Since the report of the committee does go some way towards giving a fair hearing and a proper trial, that recommendation in the committee's report is to be welcomed. We must during this war vindicate and glorify our democratic institutions; anything which tends to undermine the confidence in our democratic institutions is subversive, whether that undermining is done consciously or unconsciously, by those in power or by those who are suffering under depressed conditions.
The work of the committee was worth while. We had different points of view represented, but I think at all times every member of the committee gave the opposing point of view full and sympathetic consideration. I was glad to be a member of such a committee. While there were differences in our approach to the problem, which of course coloured the report-for a report must always be a majority decision-yet I am thoroughly convinced that if the main recommendations now made are put into effect something will be done to liberalize the administration of the defence of Canada regulations.

Mr.. Speaker, as a member of this committee I should like to say a few words in connection with the report, but first I want to express my appreciation of the fact that as one of the newer members of this house I was permitted to take part in the deliberations of a committee dealing with such an important matter as the liberty of the subject. I think I can safely say that all members of the committee approached this matter with one paramount consideration in mind, namely, that the safety of the state must come first, and that the ordinary processes of criminal law, whereby a man is deemed to be innocent until proved guilty beyond any reasonable doubt in the mind of the tribunal sitting on his case, must at least for the duration of the war in connection with these cases go by the board. We are dealing with a ruthless enemy. We cannot afford to take chances, and if there is any reasonable doubt as to the loyalty of an individual, it is up to him to dispel that doubt or be subject to imprisonment or at least close observation.
The safety of the state is the first consideration; yet we must not lose sight of the fact that we are tampering with the long-cherished and dearly-won rights and liberties of the subject, and with due regard to the safety of the state we must jealously and carefully guard those rights and liberties. The rights and liberties of the subject as we understand them in a properly constituted democracy must not be limited any more than is actually and militarily necessitated by the circumstances. Certain circumstances require drastic action; but when we do interfere with these democratic rights and liberties we must not do so lightly, and, as I say, we must curtail them only to the extent actually necessary for the safety of the state. I am fearful-and of course I am expressing my individual opinion only-lest we allow these rights and liberties to be taken away from us without proper thought and without a proper realization of what we are giving up; lest we should accept too readily statements that certain regulations are required for the safety of the state without carefully examining the underlying reasons for those assertions. I suggest that we must guard against any glossing over of the possibility of injustice with the thought that, after all, these regulations are only for the duration of the war; for I suggest that we in this house must realize that it is up to us to decide what is necessary and appropriate at this time. We cannot absolve ourselves of the responsibility that is ours when we introduce regulations such as these; we must accept that responsibility and realize that if any injustices result from the regulations we as

Defence of Canada Regulations
members of the House of Commons are responsible for such injustices because we are the ones who are interfering with the rights and liberties of the subject.
In examining the effects of the regulations I sincerely suggest that each member of the house try to put himself in the position of one against whom an order has been made under the provisions of section 21, and consider the position he would be in and whether he would then believe that he had a reasonable chance of obtaining justice. In our consideration of this matter we may be inclined to be too easily influenced by the thought, "Oh, it cannot happen to us." That, Mr. Speaker, may have been just the thought that passed through the minds of some of those who are to-day in internment camps. I am not suggesting for a moment that we have not a fair-minded man in the person of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I believe he is eminently fair-minded. I am not suggesting for a moment that he has not fair-minded men as his advisers; but he might not always have them, and it is dangerous to adopt the principle that even though some of our laws do not protect the individual as completely as they might, we can depend upon the fair-mindedness of those in charge of the administration of those laws. I suggest to you, sir, that this is a dangerous principle to adopt because we must guard against even the ultraloyal and over-zealous official, and against the possibility of a narrow-minded one. I am sorry to say that I believe there are persons in this country to-day who cannot help feeling that anyone who advocates a change in the status quo is a dangerous radical, and we must guard against the possibility of putting too much power into the hands of such individuals. I say, too, that we must be very careful to avoid the possibility of the public having ground for thinking that there is an avenue open for the introduction of political persuasion or influence. In a nutshell what I am trying to say is that we must, if we possibly can, avoid regulations which reveal bureaucratic or undemocratic tendencies.
Your committee spent a great deal of time considering these regulations; so much so, as was pointed out by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) whom we were privileged to have as chairman of the committee, that we were unable to pay very much attention to the questions of naturalization and deportation. Consequently it has been recommended that a special committee be authorized at the next session of parliament to deal with these subjects.
As to the details of the recommendations, I think I can say that there was fairly general agreement; but so far as the principles involved are concerned I for one could not
agree to the retention of certain provisions of the regulations as they previously stood, and which, since they are not excluded by the amendments, are still there. I cannot concur in the policy of continuing to have the final and complete responsibility in the hands of the Minister of Justice and his advisers. Under the regulations as amended the internee is given the right to object to his internment. There is a certain time limit within which he must make his objection, and then he is given certain of the facts for the purpose of allowing him to prepare his case. Under the amendment these facts may be amplified at the hearing before the advisory committee, which is a tribunal of three under the amended regulations. The regulations provide certain other safeguards and procedure in connection with such hearings, which I need not discuss at the moment, but the suggested amendments contain a very significant provision, which I submit is fundamental, and which is contained in paragraph 10 of regulation 22, as amended by paragraph 2 of the report, which reads:
The Minister of Justice shall cause to be put before the committee all the information about such person available to the minister except such as is not in the public interest to disclose.
In other words, this committee of three is not to have all the evidence available against an internee and, consequently what is likely to happen is this. The evidence will be passed upon by the committee. The committee will decide that there is not sufficient to have the man kept in an internment camp, and will recommend accordingly. The matter is then referred1 to the Minister of Justice through his advisers. Further evidence is furnished to him, and, as a result of that further evidence, he determines that the man should be kept incarcerated. To the bewilderment of those who do not know the man, despite the fact that the committee of three set up under the regulations has recommended his release, the minister, on information not available to that committee, determines that the person in question should be kept in an internment camp. I suggest therefore that even under these regulations as amended the committee has no responsibility.
I know it will be pointed out that in a recent report placed before the house the minister accepted all the recommendations of the committee. That is true. But it must be remembered that in a report tabled some time ago, out of twenty-five recommendations for release the minister refused to accept nine.
I suggest first of all that if the committee is going to deal with this matter in a responsible manner it is entitled to have all the evidence. It is a responsible committee and

Defence of Canada Regulations
could hear evidence in secret. There would be no necessity to have the internee present when evidence which might be prejudicial, if it leaked out, was made available. I do suggest however that unless the committee has the whole of the evidence, the set-up is useless, because we would have built up a structure which turned out to be a hollow shell. The tribunal is not yet to have all the evidence, consequently it cannot possibly give a decision in accordance with all the facts.
In addition to placing before the committee all the evidence available, I suggest it should have the final responsibility, at least in respect of cases concerning which the committee makes a unanimous finding. It may be that where there is not unanimous opinion in the committee, and consequently a doubt, final decision should be made by the minister. I suggest however, always having in mind the thought that the committee would receive all the evidence, that in cases in which the committee is unanimous in respect of a man's release, its recommendation should be taken as mandatory.
In connection with the original internment under section 21, I suggest that more formal procedure should be adopted. There should be a committee of three, such as has been suggested this morning, which would examine the evidence and advise the minister before an order is actually made. We must realize that once a man has been interned under the provisions of section 21, despite his innocence and his subsequent release a stigma attaches to him which renders it very difficult for him to reestablish himself in civil life. I believe examples could be cited to substantiate the statement I make, namely, that a man has the greatest difficulty in reestablishing himself in civil life once he has spent any time at all in an internment camp. Many people, following such internment, are inclined to believe that if he served some time in such a camp, despite his subsequent release there must have been some good reason for his internment.
Generally speaking it may be true to say that we are following the procedure as laid down in England. We have often boasted of our own autonomy, and in this instance I suggest it is up to us to adopt our own procedure, and to do it on our own responsibility. It is not necessary for us blindly to accept the procedure as laid down in England, because the situation over there is entirely different. They are in the front line of battle. I believe it can be said with safety that the regulations in England to-day have engendered much unfavourable comment on the part of responsible persons. Injustices and inequities have arisen in great numbers, and I believe that

before long-this is my personal reaction from what I have read-we shall find that the whole principle upon which the regulations in Great Britain are founded will be changed.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of this year's committee on the defence of Canada regulations I should like to make one or two observations. May I say first that the work of the committee itself was an extreme pleasure. It was one of the most harmonious committees on which I have had the privilege of serving in the past few years. While there were some details concerning which lion, members differed, such differences were indicated in a happy spirit.
In passing may I pay tribute to the management of the committee under its worthy chairman, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud). If in Canada there has been any criticism of the defence of Canada regulations, I believe it may be said that at least some of such criticism has been based upon a lack of understanding. Serving on that committee I learned many things I had not known before, and it occurred to me that if the people of Canada were permitted to learn some of the points which were brought to rny attention, it would be in the public interest. For instance, one of the criticisms levelled against the regulations is that there has been extreme delay between the picking up of a suspect and the taking of the examination. We had some reason to believe that at one time there was justification for that criticism. When the facts in that connection were known they set our minds at rest, at least'to some extent. The public should recognize that perhaps for the most part the delay was due to the fact that when war broke out, and when later Italy entered the war, it was only natural to expect a general rounding up of suspects, and that many would be taken into custody for fear that they might be a danger to the state. When several hundred men have to be examined, of necessity there must be some delay. But this condition should not arise at the present time. Hordes of suspects are not now being picked up; it is only the occasional one now and again. During the past year and a half since the war broke out the public have periodically become extremely concerned about this or that situation. I can remember when Germany began to invade the lowlands, when she invaded Norway, when fifth column activities were brought to our attention as they had never been before. The natural impression the public got was that the same thing might happen here, and it might in some degree; but I do not think everyone with a foreign name should have

Defence of Canada Regulations
been suspected. The result was almost tantamount to public hysteria. Complaints were made to the police, and I think the evidence will show that instead of having too many suspects, their biggest job was to weed out the complaints for which there was no foundation.
One particular case was brought to my attention. A young clergyman came from the United States to take over a charge in this country. He was of Dutch origin, some few generations back, and spelled his name with a "van". Because that was pronounced "von" and he happened to have a motion picture camera with him, the whole community became startled. This particular town happened to contain a number of grain elevators. The young clergyman had never seen such huge storage elevators before. He took some pictures, and it was soon noised around that he was carrying on fifth-column activities. Considerable damage was done to the reputation of the man, to the community and to the work he was carrying on.
The public should realize that it has some responsibility in this regard. It is all right for the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) to say, as he said a few moments ago to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), that the authorities should be informed. I admit that if anyone is in possession of information he should inform the authorities, but I do not think people should run off to the police simply because they are suspicious. That is not the right spirit to have in a country. Instead of people being calmed, the tendency is to rouse them and that is not good.
We are taught from childhood that one of the axioms of British justice is that a man shall be deemed to be innocent until he has been proven guilty. I believe that is still the rule in the administration of our criminal law. It would be well for the public to realize that the picture changes a little bit when a nation finds itself in a state of war, and espionage or fifth-column activities are likely to be extant in the country. At such times men are picked up not necessarily because they are guilty of this or that, but because they are regarded as being dangerous to the state. The order becomes reversed; the procedure is not carried on through the ordinary judicial channels. The hearing which is held is not necessarily a trial; it is more in the nature of an examination-not to prove that a man did this or that or said this or that, but to satisfy the authorities that he is a safe man to be at large, that he is not a danger to the state. If he is regarded as a danger to the state,
of necessity he must be confined. I think it would be well for the people of this country to recognize this.
Last year when I was speaking on this matter I said that it might be possible for those who are administering the defence of Canada regulations to make psychological mistakes. As someone has said, we are fighting a psychological war, and this principle enters into the administration of the defence of Canada regulations in a time of war. There is a very strong psychological principle of which the government must be aware. Personally I deplore the emphasis being placed upon the picking up of a suspect on some flimsy piece of would-be evidence while perhaps there are things taking place in the country which are far more dangerous to public thinking. I am not so sure that we did the right thing in outlawing Jehovah's Witnesses. I am not so sure that we did the right thing in outlawing Technocracy. I am not expressing my deliberate opinion, but I am saying that I am not so certain that these two organizations are a tremendous danger to the stafe. At lease the authorities should be very careful how they administer the defence of Canada regulations in respect to those two organizations. Perhaps I do not know all that I should know about them, but what I have in mind is this, that there are things happening in Canada, and, I would go so far as to include perhaps certain policies which the government itself holds, which psychologically are a greater danger to public thinking than the distribution of perhaps some more or less harmless literature by these two organizations or even by others.
Perhaps one may wonder what I have in .mind. Of course I know that the government has the answers to all these criticisms, but whether the answers are satisfactory to other members of the house or satisfactory to the public	of	Canada; I	do	not	know. Forinstance, we had brought up in the house the other	day	the matter	of	the	shipment ofwheat	in	sacks from	Canada	in Japanesebottoms, the destination of which was supposed	to	be stomewhere	in China. The
government may have its answer to that, but J am saying this, that whatever answer it gives I do not believe it has satisfied the .people of Canada, If there is anything we desire to maintain in all of Canada it is complete unity and complete loyalty. Here we are carrying on a recruiting campaign and ,a campaign to raise the victory loan, and this thing coming into the picture right now is causing dissension.
You may say, what has this to do with the defence of Canada regulations. I answer just this. An individual may be picked up somewhere in Canada for distributing a pamphlet.

The whole community becomes aroused. Yet on that very same day they read in the press a report to the effect that Canadian wheat is perhaps being shipped to the axis powers. That is extremely bad. While I am on this point may I suggest that there are others besides members of parliament, and those [DOT] who are administering the defence of Canada regulations who have a responsibility in the matter of the unity of Canada and the loyalty of its people.

It is the sort of thing that retards proper patriotism. It is the sort of thing that causes people to question their loyalty to Canada, people who want to be loyal. It is the sort of thing that plants seeds of doubt in their minds.
As the hon. member for Acadia remarks, it raises in the minds of the people a question as to the sincerity of the government in its war effort. That must be recognized, although I personally do not question its sincerity. In view of the state the country was in when the war broke out, and of what has had to be done on short order, I am not going to suggest that any other government could have done better. If any blame is to be attributed to our lack of preparation it will have to be focused upon the statesmanship of this country during the past fifteen or twenty years. It is there that the trouble lies, not necessarily in the present set-up. I shall have more to say upon that topic, which is not relevant to the defence of Canada regulations, upon some other occasion.
I was dealing with the psychological effect of these regulations as regards our war effort.
I do not suppose that at present we are shipping scrap metal to Japan; I could not prove either that we are or that we are not. But certainly we were doing so not very long ago. Now we are going out in pursuance of our salvage campaign and asking people to contribute their scrap metal. Certain farmers who have a good deal of scrap metal have commented to me along this line: "It is all very well to ask for scrap metal now, but it is a known fact that hundreds of thousands of tons were shipped to the axis powers or to Japan prior to the war, and perhaps since the war." Such things have a tremendous effect on public opinion. If we are to achieve a total war effort in this country, it will pay the government and other hon. members to be very careful, even in the minutest detail, of the way in which we carry it on, and of the effect of the defence of Canada regulations upon the mind of the people and their relation to our entire war effort.

Defence of Canada Regulations
Personally I am in favour of the adoption of this report. The recommendations contained therein are an improvement upon what we had before. I believe that the Minister of Justice has been unduly blamed for a number of things which, even though he may be responsible for them, must be viewed in the light of the fact that he is in a position which has been imposed upon him, and it is not altogether a happy one. In my opinion he has done his work exceptionally well. I can take no other attitude, not because of any compulsion upon me, but because it is my conviction that he desires to act fairly in the administration of the regulations for which he is responsible.
May I specifically call attention to the recommendation for the continuance of the work of this committee or of a similar body during the next session, and for a further and more detailed investigation with regard to naturalization, and regulations relating to the deportation of those who have come under the odium of the defence of Canada regulations.

speechtext:
Previous speakers in this debate have all emphasized the importance of this matter, and, in my submission, quite properly so, because it concerns two subjects of the utmost importance to all of us at this time, namely, the safety of the state, and the liberty of the subject. Wrapped up in those two subjects is the whole reason why we are fighting this war, and in their relation lies the difference between ourselves and the system for which we are fighting, and the system of nazi Germany.
The subject is important for another reason. It is not only necessary that laws should be just; it is equally necessary that they should be recognized as just. Owing partly to the fact that this subject has not been discussed very much in parliament there has grown up a considerable amount of misunderstanding and misapprehension about the defence of Canada regulations and the way in which they operate. The best way to clear up that misapprehension and convey understanding and confidence is by debate in this house. It is interesting to note that in the British house, despite their natural preoccupation with the war, this subject is probably more fully discussed than any other single subject outside the conduct of
the war itself, and that in Britain parliamentary concurrence is required in every change made in the regulations.
The defence of Canada regulations are designed to promote the safety of Canada. We are in a war for survival, and it is impossible to overestimate or exaggerate the great seriousness of the situation in which we and our allies find ourselves. We know that the enemy has used every means in every country to accomplish his fell designs. We have seen the long roll of countries that have been pulled down to slavery by ruthless aggression and propaganda and fifth-column activities- Austria, Memel, Danzig, Poland, Norway, Denmark, Holland, Belgium, France, Roumania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Yugoslavia, Greece. We have seen what happened there, and we do not intend that it shall happen here.
The defence of Canada regulations are as much designed to defend us in what we are doing in this country as are the munitions of war with which we arm our troops. They are a fighting weapon, and for that purpose they are being used. Unless Canada is kept free, the freedom of Canadians is not worth anything.
I intend to deal principally with regulations 21 and 22. Regulation 21 provides that the Minister of Justice, if satisfied that with a view to preventing any particular person from acting in any manner prejudicial to the public safety or the safety of the state it is necessary so to do, may issue an order for his detention. The words "acting in any manner prejudicial to the public safety or the safety of the state" are abstract, but if we substitute for them "the safety of Canada," the place in which we live, the place we love, then the people of Canada would recognize more the purpose and need of the regulations.
Detention is not ordered by reason of the commission of any offence. It is not a criminal proceeding; it is purely precautionary and preventive. The purpose of the regulation is to render harmless any person who might reasonably be suspected of plotting to cause harm to the state. Some critics of the regulations suggest that we should "be tough," that we should lock them all up. But who is to tell who "they" are that we should lock up? That is the purpose of the regulations and of the procedure.	_
Other critics of the regulations say that the procedure should be judicial, that the whole thing should be assimilated to a trial before a court. But the great mass of the people, and surely all hon. members, recognize that the prime purpose of the regulation is to protect the safety of the state, the safety of Canada,

Defence of Canada Regulations
the defence of Canada; and it is of paramount importance that that purpose should come first in all our considerations.
Second, it is the responsibility of the government of Canada to take all means that may be necessary to secure the safety of the state. That responsibility rests squarely on the shoulders of the government, and the government cannot divest itself of this responsibility by turning it over to any court. No Minister of Justice would feel obliged to follow the recommendations of anyone else. The responsibility falls upon the government; the government must have power to discharge the responsibility, and that of necessity involves that the final discretion as to who should be detained must rest with the Minister of Justice. I suppose everyone here recognizes that no one would b more pleased than the Minister of Justice himself to be relieved of that responsibility-

speechtext:
Of necessity it must be administrative, but he will naturally exercise that function with discretion and in as judicial a manner as he possibly can.
I submit that the procedure cannot be completely judicial. Also that by reason of the very character of the whole operation and the purpose of the regulations there are some matters that cannot be disclosed to any court or to any body. The identity of informers, the sources of information must be kept back by the minister and his officers when they feel that it would not be in the public interest to disclose such sources of information, because once the source is disclosed it is no longer available for the purposes for which it might be used.
I submit, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that there are three principles to which we should subscribe. First comes the paramount consideration of the safety and defence of Canada.
[Mr. Claxton.J
Then comes the responsibility of the government, and third, the fact that of necessity the matter cannot be dealt with in a completely judicial manner.
These things having been said, we come to a matter of the utmost importance; that is, that we should do everything in our power to secure to every individual his liberty and to see to it that no man is detained longer than is absolutely necessary to achieve the primary purpose I have mentioned. That is so for a very important reason. This is not only a war for the survival of nations; it is a war for the survival of ideas and ideals. How we are to fight the war depends on morale as much as anything else, and morale to a great extent is wrapped up with this question of individual liberty, with our fighting as free men and not as slaves. Dorothy Thompson put this magnificently in commenting on the president's speech last month, when she said:
And then he sat down with us and said, it seemed, "I know you want to know how things are-well, they are like this."
And .listening, we knew they are like this. Just exactly like this. When he stopped speaking, we -were quiet, and then suddenly we felt happy.-happy and free.
That is the function of free speech. To make people more free. To take shackles off their minds and off their wills; to bring light into their intelligences, understanding into their hearts, and to put marrow into their bones.
In those words she put the case for freedom, and it works. Freedom is the most important thing in the world, the breath of life, the source of all security, the means of all progress. To assert that liberty is dead is the same thing as saying that life itself is dead. So much is this so that every person speaking of our war and what we are fighting for says we are fighting for freedom. The words have been repeated over and over again, until somehow they are beginning to lose their force with some of us and are coming to be just words. It is important that we should put the words into acts, that we should act them as we go along and show that we believe freedom is important by pursuing freedom as a way of life to-day, as well as a goal of war and the fruit of victory. We must convince our workers that our interest in democracy begins at home.
Then, too, we must differentiate just as much as possible between ourselves and the enemy we are fighting. We can beat them with more democracy, not less; with more freedom and not more naziness. When we say "he should be shut up"; when we raise a race cry of any kind; when we speak about leadership as though it is some divine principle, then we are playing Hitler's game, we are showing that we also are a little hitlerized.

Defence of Canada Regulations
We have to make our democracy fight for us, and we have to fight with it as we go along. This is important in Canada by reason of our alien population, with some 800,000 people of German descent and 140,000 of Italian descent. It is of the utmost importance that we should show these people, the vast majority of whom are completely loyal, that they were right in leaving the old land and coming to this country; that they were right in staking their future here; that this is the place where they can be free to work out their lives in cooperation with us and have the protection of our laws.
Then we must observe free ways because of the effect on neutral countries. Sometimes in the United States we see some of the enemies of our cause, as well as others who sincerely believe in isolation, stoutly maintaining that if the United States goes to war she loses her freedom. We in Canada have shown that this is not so, and we should continue to show it.
There is the effect of our freedom on the enemy himself. Every time we bring about any curtailment of individual liberty Hitler uses that fact in his propaganda machine. Ultimately the break-down of the enemy will be brought about by the recognition by his people that in ours they can find a very much better way of life than in any nazi system.
A further point is that repression and suppression create fear and lack of confidence. We should not repress our friends; we should suppress Hitler. There is also the question of the possible misuse of arbitrary power. I think everyone is agreed, as all the representations made to our committee agreed, that we have no reason to fear this under the present Minister of Justice. They seemed to suggest that under some other minister, who might be one of the bon. gentlemen sitting opposite, there might be some such cause for fear, but there is always the possibility of abuse in any restrictions on liberty; and the 'best safeguard against such abuse is liberty itself and the freedom to criticize and speak one's own mind.
Throughout the war we have done everything in our power to keep our money worth exactly what it was when we went into the war. By avoiding inflation We have done our utmost to preserve material values. We should also do our utmost to preserve spiritual values, because they are what we are fighting for.
I, think that in considering the regulations and the representations that were made our committee was moved by consideration such as I have described to the house. That is, the committee had in mind the paramount necessity of safeguarding the security of Canada
and then of doing everything not inconsistent with that end to safeguard the liberty of the individual. And i't is fair to say that in our deliberations, as well as in the submissions made to us, there was shown a very wide feeling that, generally speaking, the regulations were being fairly administered, without very great hardship. It was shown that they were necessary, but that naturally everything possible should be done to safeguard the rights of the individual, once the security of the state had been obtained.
The representations regarding regulation 22 really came under five heads. First, it was suggested that if possible we should have some formal proceeding before the alien was interned. I confess I should have liked to see that done, had it been possible to work out something acceptable to the committee. I spent a great deal of time trying to draft something, and I am sure other hon. members did likewise, and we found that we could not do it. It is an exceedingly difficult problem. There is also this to be said, that if this proceeding were mandatory on the minister it might prevent his taking the action we would want him to take without delay. And if it is not mandatory, but rather discretionary, then it would add nothing to the present situation. In that connection I personally express the hope that the minister may find it possible to seek the advice of three persons appointed by himself in all cases when detention is recommended instead of just in respect of persons of enemy origin.
The second complaint was that the detained persons did not have sufficient particulars put before them to enable them to make their defence. We found that the particulars were often very brief, and it will be seen that in the suggested regulation 22, the adoption of which is recommended, there is provision for the fullest possible particulars not inconsistent with the public interest.
Third, complaints were made on grounds of delay. We found that there had been delays, but that they had arisen almost of necessity from the fact that last June and July large numbers of people of Italian origin were apprehended in a hurry. That had to be done, and some time was required in which to dispose of their cases. Provisions will be found in the suggested regulations which have for their purpose the cutting down of delays.
Fourth, it has been suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) that all evidence available to the minister should be put before the committee. I believe it is the view of the majority of members that that is not possible in every case, and that it

Defence of Canada Regulations
is not in the public interest to disclose all the evidence or all the sources of information the minister may have.
Finally, it is suggested-and it was repeated a few minutes ago in the question of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson)-that the minister should have to follow the advice of the advisory committee.

speechtext: I shall attempt to answer the leader of the opposition on that point. I would submit to him this case: The advisory committee brings in a report recommending release. The minister has available to him information from a secret source which he did not feel at liberty to put before the committee. He may then exercise his discretion, and, notwithstanding the recommendations, refuse to accept the advice of the advisory committee.

speechtext:
Then why
have an advisory committee at all?

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Because the advisory committee is of the utmost assistance in dealing with the vast majority of cases. The number of cases in which the minister has refused to follow the advice of the advisory committee is exceedingly small. I believe I am correct when I say that it is considerably under twenty since the outbreak of the war. And even in those cases I understand the minister keeps the facts dontinually under review. They come up again and again. The minister in these cases has exercised his discretion and has not ordered the immediate release of the aliens.
In the report submitted to the house a new regulation 22 has been suggested for adoption by the governor in council. It describes in much greater detail than before the suggested lines of procedure, a procedure which is much more liberal than that now followed in Great Britain. The procedure we had before was somewhat similar to that followed in Great Britain. That which we hope the government will introduce in consequence of this report is fairer, and provides ampler safeguards and a better chance to the detained person than the procedure we had before, or that followed in Great Britain.
I would draw to the attention of the house the fact that while criticizing the report in part, hon. members who have spoken previously have all agreed that it represents a [Mr. Claitoo-i
substantial improvement on the situation which existed before. I believe that is the view of every fair-minded person who reads the report. And it does not in any single particular reduce the safety of Canada. From that point of view it leaves the position exactly as it was. But it does add safeguards to the procedure which already exists.	>
In addition to the defence of Canada regulations we have the provisions of the criminal code and the Treachery Act. There is ample power in Canada to deal with subversive elements and subversive activities That is shown by the fact that since the beginning of the war, so far as I know, there has been no single act of sabotage in Canada traceable to enemy origin. That does not mean that we may not have such acts; it does not mean that we should become over-confident or complacent, but it does mean that we have taken the measures necessary to safeguard Canada during this time of war, and that they have been effective.
In addition to such measures, however, may I point out to the house that far more effective than any repressive means is the loyalty of the Canadian people, the morale of the Canadian people. All the persons who have been prosecuted for so-called beer-parlour offences under regulation 39 may have done less harm to recruiting in Canada than a single newspaper editorial. We cannot deal with newspaper editorials by regulation. No one would wish us to. But we can secure the cooperation of the editor and the Canadian people, through every possible means. We can strengthen our pride in Canada and its achievements. We can strengthen our sense of individual responsibility, and our confidence in our institutions. We can strengthen our belief in victory and should be able to hope that after victory we shall have a better world. What kind of world are we fighting for? We are not fighting for a world in which, after the war, we shall have another depression. This is found in "Canada Fights." We are fighting for-

a world in which a nation would not be called upon to go to war every fifteen or twenty years; a world in which wheat and other agricultural commodities, together with the product of forest and mine, could he sold at a price that would enable the producer to live in reasonable comfort and to educate his children; a world in which every adult able and willing to work would have employment, and in which our present liberties of thought, speech and religion would be maintained.
I suggest that those are war aims to which every party in this house, every hon. member in this house can subscribe. These, or similar aims, should be proclaimed throughout the land as the reason why we are fighting. We are not fighting just to keep the status quo, to

Defence of Canada Regulations
retain our membership in good clubs, to keep our money; we are fighting a far more desperate struggle than that, and we are going to be able to put our utmost into it only if we have some such aim, only if we can show that we can plan a better world than Hitler, only if we can create a common goal of living and give life a new meaning. These are practical considerations to-day, the kind of thing that the Canadian people can be told again and again. The text for the telling might well be taken from I Corinthians, chapter 14, the eighth verse:
For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?
Every agency in Canada can strengthen our pride, our confidence, our belief, our faith and our fortitude to endure united until victory and peace are won. With this kind of feeling in the land there will not be much need for defence of Canada regulations.
To-day in Montreal we hear two different kinds of rumours about recruiting. These are being spread about to create racial feeling among the English and the French. People who hear these rumours should stop them because there is not a particle of truth in them. Every hon. member has heard rumours which are spread irresponsibly. We are having a black-out in Montreal to-night, and I suggest that we should have a black-out of rumours and a black-out of unfounded criticism for the next three or four weeks. We would then see what effect it would have upon the war loan, upon recruiting and upon the feelings of the whole country. I remember during the last war in France toward the middle of July, 1918, an order was issued calling upon the troops of the Canadian corps to stop repeating rumours which had been spreading like wildfire. That order was effective and the spirit of the troops changed within a week or two. We then moved down to Amiens and started the battle which ended the war. I suggest that the same kind of thing should be done to-day by the Canadian people.
We should remember that we are the democrats who are going to show that democracy is the best system, not Shakespeare, not Milton, not Burke, not Washington and not Lincoln, We are the ones who have to show that we can fight through to victory. This building is a monument which reminds us of other hard days through which we fought to victory:
Read how free men throughout this land kept faith in the hour of trial and in the day of battle, remembering the traditions they had been taught, counting life nothing without liberty.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate, but as I was one of the original members of the committee which was set up last year, and also of the subcommittee, I feel called upon to make a few observations. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) has said both last year and this year the members of the committee were highly pleased with the work of the committee. I thought that last year we had a perfect committee, but this year's committee was at least as good. Every member was seized of the importance and seriousness of the job he had to do. In this respect I must pay tribute to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). He is doing a job which he d~>s not like any more than any of us liked the work we had to do on this committee. But no other course can be followed. We must have laws and the final say as to the administration of the laws and regulations and the security of our country must be with the Minister of Justice. I cannot think of any way in which the government can be relieved of its responsibility in connection with the security of the country.
Mention has been made of the fact that there has not been one act of sabotage in Canada which could be traced to enemy agents. I attribute that to the defence of Canada regulations and a very efficient Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The mounted police have done a job which would be a credit to any police force. This year the regulations have been liberalized to quite a considerable extent and with few exceptions the recommendations made by the committee have been unanimous. The differences which did exist were not very great.
I wish to pay a tribute to the previous speakers who I think have stated the case clearly and in a worthwhile manner. As I see it, the difficulty has been in deciding how far the rights of the individual should be restricted in order to protect the security of the state. By amending the regulations we have demonstrated to the Canadian people that we appreciated their point of view in the exceptions they took to certain of the regulations. In the main we have modified the provisions which they felt were obnoxious.
Comment has been made throughout the country about the interning of labour leaders. I for one am quite willing to take the word of the Minister of Justice that these men were interned not because they were labour leaders but because they were communists. I am positive that no labour leader need have the slightest fear about carrying on his legitimate

Defence of Canada Regulations
duties; he need have no fear about any action which the Minister of Justice might take under the defence of Canada regulations.
The previous speakers have covered the ground thoroughly and I wish to pay tribute to them. If we should find from experience that these regulations should be further liberalized or tightened up, time and events will show and we shall have another opportunity next year to iron out any difficulties that we may have with them between now and then.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was one of the members of the special committee that was appointed to consider and review the defence of Canada regulations. I voted in favour of the recommendations that were made by that committee. Its report speaks for itself, and as practically all, but not quite all, the members who have taken part in this debate have expressed themselves in favour of these recommendations, there is very little I wish to say at the present time.
While some changes have been recommended in the report, they do not materially alter the regulations now in force. Having listened to the evidence that was taken by the committee, and compared the regulations with the recommendations that have been made, I am of the opinion that all the recommendations are of a minor nature and that there has been no deviation from the principles which have been followed in the past. The recommendations, if adopted, may improve, but perhaps only to a very slight extent, the regulations as they stand at present. There will not be, and perhaps there is no need for, any substantial improvement. The recommendations will neither alter the underlying principles on which the regulations are based, nor weaken their effectiveness.
The most important recommendation has to do with regulation 22. The recommendation provides that when an internee objects to being interned his objection will be heard by a committee of three. This committee is to be appointed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and is to consist of a judge and two other persons. The committee at the present time consists of one person, a judge of a high court. The advisory committee-and you will note that in the regulations it is called an advisory committee-has very limited powers. It has the right to take evidence and to hear the objections made by the person who is interned, and after taking this evidence it advises or makes a recommendation to the minister. It has no greater power than that. The minister does not have to accept its recommendation. The

minister may if he sees fit act on its recommendation, but if he does not see fit, the person may remain interned.
The important principle underlying this regulation is the principle, if I may express it crudely or roughly, of government responsibility. The government is responsible for the conduct of this war, and these regulations are a part, and not an unimportant part, of our war effort. Responsibility for the enforcement of these regulations must in my opinion rest with the government, just as much as carrying on the rest of our war effort is the government's responsibility. Under these regulations great power is placed in the hands of the Minister of Justice as a member of the government, and the final responsibility rests with the government.
It has been suggested that this power be taken out of the hands of the Minister of Justice and that a judicial tribunal be set up in place of the advisory committee. The judicial tribunal would consider objections raised by the internee, would hold a form of trial and take evidence, and its decision would be final-or rather some people have suggested that it should be final only if the decision of the judicial committee was unanimous, otherwise the final decision should rest with the Minister of Justice. But the responsibility for the administration of the regulations would be in this judicial committee, not in the government, and there would be no appeal from its decision.
In my opinion the responsibility for the enforcement and administration of these regulations must rest with the government. It is on that principle that this recommendation has been made to the house, a recommendation with which I concur.
