Mr. Speaker, just a brief word. I happen to be one of those who vigorously opposed retaining ini the criminal code section 98, and I would oppose it to-day, 'because it certainly denies the right of the individual to a fair trial. The defence of Canada regulations, amendments to which we are now considering, did n'ot suit me any too well either, but I must say that I welcome the improvements which have been recommended by the special committee. I am well pleased with its work ,and its report, and, like the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon), I say that if the amended regulations are found not to work out well in practice, the committee can go to work again next year and amend them again. The members of the committee are to be commended for the time they have given to their work and the intelligent service they have rendered. I heartily

Defence of Canada Regulations
welcome the report, because with the adoption of these recommendations it seems to me that the individual will have more of a right 'to an honest trial before he can be whisked away.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would I think be presumptuous if I were t'o make any extended remarks on this report at this late stage of the session. If one were disposed to think that we are endeavouring to close the session he would not get very much evidence of it from the extended debate which has taken place on this resolution, and perhaps I should not rise at all. On both occasions in the last session when this matter was under review I expressed the opinion that the paramount principle underlying this system of handling subversive elements in the community is the safety of the state. The second is that the government has the responsibility. The only question that has ever been in my mind has been the method employed and we may have had and I suppose still will have very divergent views with regard to what is the best method. I do not think there is much difference of opinion on the two questions of principle to which I have alluded.
I do not intend to go seriatim through the various recommendations of the committee. Some of them are of importance and some of them are not. There are just one or two observations which I would like to make, however, anterior to a short review of the recommendations; they arise out of the remarks made this morning by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), in which he chastised all those who had anything to do with the conditions in pre-war Europe, even mentioning the name of Mr. Neville Chamberlain.
It is all very well, after the event, to condemn Mr. Chamberlain or to condemn Munich, but I venture to say that there are millions of people on this continent and in England who welcomed Munich and the declaration of Munich, based as it was on the fundamental principle that nations are expected to respect their word of honour. Mr. Chamberlain was not the first man-and I suggest that, as long as Hitler lives and carries on, he will not be the last one-to be deceived by the word of that dictator. I am astonished that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar should have found fault with the regime existent in England prior to the declaration of war, because I recall that it is not so many years ago that his leader visited soviet Russia and was received with open arms by the soviet government. Let that not be forgotten in Canada.

I do hope that the leader of the opposition -

speechtext:
I bow
immediately, Mr. Speaker, to your ruling. I may say that I had concluded all the observations I desired to make in that connection, and I shall now proceed with the speech I had intended to make.
The main feature of the report is the clearer definition of the procedure to be followed by a detained person in presenting objections to his detention. I think that that is a constructive part of the report. In that respect it will not, I assume, meet with the approval of all those who have taken objection to what has been termed the rather peremptory procedure at present existing, but in my view, having analysed the recommendations as best I may, and, I may remark, cursorily, the report constitutes a considerable advance in that regard.
To my mind there are two main features of the report, in which the following principles are adopted.
In the first place, immediately a person is detained he is not whirled away into an internment camp. There are cases, of course, in which that might be justified. There are cases in which, I believe, it has been demonstrated that it is amply justified. I recall to mind what occurred in the dying days of the sitting of this house in August last, and I have yet to hear anybody condemn what took place here and what took place out of this house. To-day it is proposed that any detained person shall be kept in a local gaol under similar conditions to a person awaiting trial, until his objection has been disposed of or until he indicates that he proposes to make no objection. That, I think, is an advance; it is fair and just, and I approve it.
The second principle incorporated in the recommendations is that as soon as possible a person detained is to be informed of the general grounds on which he is detained, and notice of his detention is to be given to hia family, where possible and not contrary to the public interest. It is difficult to conceive of a condition where it would not be in the public interest to inform a man's family of the fact of his detention, I do not go any farther than that, but the fact that a man has been detained should, as a matter of course, be communicated to his family.

Defence of Canada Regulations
Otherwise a person so detained would be held incommunicado; and I suggest that there would be ground for serious objection thereto. As to the reasons for his detention, that is another matter.
The report goes on to indicate that an objection to detention may be filed within thirty days. That is to say, a person detained has a right to demand a hearing, and the matter is then referred to an advisory committee.
Fourth, the Minister of Justice is empowered to appoint one or more advisory committees, to consist of three persons, the chairman of which must hold or have held judicial office. The only departure there is that, instead of being referred to one person who holds or has held high judicial position, it is to be referred to a committee of three, one of whom is occupying or has occupied a judicial position. I am wondering why the word "high" has been eliminated from the recommendation. This is an important matter. The liberty of the subject is involved, and under the laws of Canada, only high court judges deal with questions arising out of th application for writ of habeas corpus. We have in the jurisdiction of New Brunswick, with which I am familiar, another procedure, not based on the issue of the writ itself, but on what is termed an order of the nature of a habeas corpus the jurisdiction under which may be exercised by a county court judge. But under this recommendation it would be possible for a police or stipendiary magistrate to be appointed the chairman of the advisory committee. I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that that is not good enough. Where the liberty of the subject is involved, the chairman of the committee should be a person holding or Who has held a high judicial position. There is no reason why that should not be. It has been the practice in the past, and I recommend to the right hon. gentleman that he follow that practice in the future.
The fifth recommendation is, as I understand it, that the chairman shall be required to inform the objector within a reasonable time before hearing of the grounds on which he is held and to furnish him with particulars of the reason for his detention as, in the opinion of the chairman, circumstances permit. That is to say, the chairman is required to inform the accused-if I may use that term
of the nature of the charge against him. This is common British justice, and should be done, and as fully as possible, so that there may be sufficient opportunity of defence. It is I think impossible to have what we understand in criminal law as full right of

defence in cases of this kind, but there should be as much right of defence and of answer as the circumstances permit.
Then it is provided that at the hearing "such particulars shall be further supplemented by giving the objector, all such further particulars as the committee shall deem necessary and advisable." Of course that leaves the discretion in the committee. Why it is restricted to what the committee deem advisable has not so far developed, unless it be from the remarks delivered in the course of his address this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) that there may be occasions when it is not in the public interest that this should be done. Conceivably that is true. No one has suggested a concrete illustration, but I am willing in the interests of the paramount principle to have it restricted that far. But I point out that this is not full right of defence.
Then the next move forward, if I may so term it, is that the objector may be represented by counsel. I do not recall what has been the practice in the past. I had thought there was the right to be represented by counsel. It seems to me, however, that if heretofore that right has not been given, this is an extension of a principle which all of us can support.
A new provision is made whereby a person objecting to a censorship order of the Secretary of State may lodge his protest with a committee appointed by the Minister of Justice, such committee to consist of a person who holds or has held high judicial office. Hon. gentlemen will observe that the principle of granting a hearing before a committee and the retention of the status of a high judicial officer is maintained here, whereas it is not maintained in the case of detained persons. I am at a loss to know why there is the distinction in this case, which is of much less importance than in the former case to which I alluded a little earlier. Here you are dealing with a censorship order made by the Secretary of State; there you are dealing with the liberty of the individual himself. It seems to me that if in one case you have a high judicial officer carrying out this function, there is that much more reason why you should have a high judicial officer presiding in the other case. I recommend that to the Minister of Justice. Why two separate types of committee should be contemplated I am not aware, but I do suggest that in the second case, where there is objection to a censorship order from the Secretary of State, one person is quite sufficient, because in that case where he is sitting alone the person must be one who holds or has held high judicial office.

Defence of Canada Regulations
A committee of one person who holds or has held high judicial office reviews the censorship order. I have pointed out what appears to be an anomaly, and I conceive that my duty in that regard has been accomplished.
Then it is to be noted that under regulation 21 (3) the Minister of Justice is required at the beginning of each session of parliament and each four weeks thereafter during the session to make a report to parliament showing, among other things, the number of cases in which he has refused to follow the advice of an advisory committee. I suggest that in so doing the minister is exercising a judicial function, notwithstanding the statement to the contrary by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and that this is not a mere ministerial duty that the minister is performing. If it is exercised on this basis there can of course be no objection to the minister reviewing the proceedings, and in so doing he must exercise a judicial function. If it is merely an administrative matter, of course he does not look beyond the evidence that has been submitted to the advisory committee.	Presumably he may have other
evidence, but in considering that other evidence he is exercising a judicial function. Of course this may be a mere academic discussion and not worth while at the moment, but I submit there is a clear distinction and the distinction should be recognized.
If the Minister of Justice under regulation 21 (3) is required to make a report to parliament, why should not the Secretary of State in the case of a censorship order be required to make a similar report with respect to the number of instances in which he has refused to follow the advice of the proposed new committee which is to hear objections against censorship orders? I suggest that to my hon. friend the Secretary of State. And also that there should be incorporated in the new regulations setting up this new committee on censorship the provision that there should be a report to parliament in those cases just as in the cases of detained persons by the Minister of Justice. It seems to me that if parliament is to know the number in the one case it should know the number in the other. And in the case of the censorship order parliament should know what the causes are and why orders have been made. There is no reason in the world similar to that which I really believe applies to the other case of which the minister spoke on one former occasion, that is the high interest of the state. I commend that suggestion to the Secretary of State.
Then there is a third recommendation, which has not been alluded to to-day and which may not be of paramount importance, namely 14873-232}
that consideration be given to segregating in separate places of detention the different classes of persons detained under regulation 21. Presumably enemy aliens, communists, national unity party members and so forth are referred to. What are the implications of this recommendation? I really do not understand the effect of it. There should be some elucidation.
Another matter the committee recommends is that the Minister of Justice give consideration to the advisability of making a regulation under which the sale of ammunition for pistols and revolvers shall be prohibited until the purchaser has produced his registration certificate for the pistol or revolver. This is an excellent recommendation. It would assist the police in checking up on the registration of fireams. Doubtless there are many firearms in this country of which the police know nothing.
Then the committee recommends that for the duration of the war a special committee of the house should be appointed at each session to consider and review the defence of Canada regulations. I hope the government will adopt this suggestion.
The committee has performed from the beginning a useful function. The work of the committee has been carried on, I believe, with thoroughness. An exchange of views by intelligent men around a committee table free from publicity, where men can speak their thoughts, will I believe in the end evolve the very best possible system.
It is a matter of regret to me that the committee found that it could not deal at this session with the question of the laws relating to naturalization and deportation. There are many aspects of the law relating to naturalization and deportation which require careful study and scrutiny, and I hope that next session such an opportunity will be provided. If it is considered that the work of the committee on the regulations themselves is too great and too heavy, then it would be worth while giving consideration to the setting up of a separate special committee. One of the things this committee could do, one of the matters to which the minister referred in moving concurrence in this report, and something which, in my judgment, could be done with great advantage, would be to study whether the provisions of the Immigration Act as it now exists are adequate to deal with what probably will be a very 1 arge number of applications for entry into Canada when the war concludes. It is all very well to visualize this country as an asylum for the oppressed. We are willing to aid and succour those who are oppressed, but we have made mistakes in our immigration policy in the past; the government and everyone else knows

Defence of Canada Regulations
that. I think we must continue to have regulated entry into this country after the war; otherwise we might find ourselves in a plight which to-day we would not appreciate.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), I do not wish to delay the adoption of this report, but I think I owe it to the house and more particularly to the members who served on this committee to say at least a few words in appreciation of their work. I desire to express not only my congratulations but also my thanks, and the thanks of the house, to the members of this special committee for the work they have done and for the study and attention they have given to that work. I do not think I should speak on the various recommendations which have been made, and which have been discussed during the course of this debate, except to say that I will see to it that these recommendations are immediately incorporated in the defence of Canada regulations and that those matters which are recommended to the consideration of the government are given that consideration.
What I wish to say is rather on the general aspect of the question, which is a very difficult one. As I have stated already in connection with this matter, there are two schools of thought as to what should be done, which schools differ materially. At the beginning of hostilities those who wanted to intern the largest possible number of persons who might be suspected were rather in the majority; the demand was for the internment of many people, and the blame or criticism was that too many were left at liberty. A little later there was a reversal in the trend of public opinion, and the criticism was that there were too many people interned, that civil liberty was endangered. To-day the two schools are still working, and I am continually receiving complaints of the most contradictory nature. For instance, members of the civil liberty league write me that we are much too strict in keeping people interned who might be released. At the same time I am in receipt of resolutions adopted by various branches of the Canadian Legion stating that too many interned people have been released, that sufficient care is not being exercised, and that this is a dangerous condition. I have also received letters and resolutions with regard to labour leaders who have been interned. Of course there are no labour leaders interned as such, but only those who secured admission to labour unions while more particularly concerned about the propagation of communist doctrines. At the same time I am in receipt of requests that some of the labour organizers,

particularly those coming from the country to our south, should be treated as disturbing influences in our country, and that strict action should be taken with regard to them.
To show hon. members how different the views are, last week I received a letter from a gentleman protesting violently against certain speeches and writings of another gentleman, and blaming me and the government for not interning him as an enemy to the security of the state at this time. At the very moment I was reading this letter a report was submitted to me by the police suggesting that it might be advisable to intern the gentleman who had written me the letter, for being an agitator and an enemy of the state.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: It would be interesting to know who were these gentlemen.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Of course I cannot give the names, but perhaps the gentleman who wrote me the letter will be able to identify himself.
I desire to repeat what I have stated already in this house, particularly in answer to the criticism that some of the internees are not given a fair trial, as in criminal cases. These men are not interned as a punitive measure, as though they had committed some crime. If that were the situation, before they could be convicted and sentenced there would have to be complete evidence; there would have to be a fair trial, and they would have to be given the benefit of the doubt. This, however, is not a punitive action; it is a preventive action, for the safety of the state. It is the action of a nation at war, that has to protect itself against any possibility of people doing something which might harm or injure the war effort of the nation. That is why keeping the final discretion in the Minister of Justice is, I believe, the only thing that could be done, and that is where I differ from my good friend the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) who made a fine speech to-day on this matter. I do not think it would be advisable to place upon a judge the responsibility of deciding whether or not a man who might be dangerous to the safety of the state during a war should be interned. It is more a matter of public safety and public policy. After all, as the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) has said, it is the government which is responsible for the safety of the state. This is a serious and disagreeable responsibility, but it cannot be avoided.
On certain occasions I have worried a good deal about what should be done. If the judge, after having heard witnesses, consisting of the

Defence of Canada Regulations
family of the interned man, and some others, comes to the conclusion .that the man is not a serious danger and should be released, and if the men responsible for order, the officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and especially those whom I trust and in whose judgment I have confidence, tell me on their responsibility that they do not wish to be held responsible for what that man could do if he were left at liberty; then, if I order the release of such a man, and a month or two after such release a serious act of sabotage is committed, resulting in loss of life, and if such activities can be traced to the man in question, who would be responsible? I would be. The government would be. The judge, for whose judgment I would have the greatest respect, would not be the one who would be blamed. No; the Minister of Justice would be blamed. The government would be blamed. And it is not only a question of blame, but the feeling that in some degree my country might suffer because that man is free.
That is why in some instances I could not bring my mind to an acceptance of recommendations for release. However disagreeable it may be, I believe I am more completely fulfilling my duty to Canada when I keep such a man inside.
I believe the recommendation for a committee of three instead of a committee of one is a good one. The leader of the opposition has said that he cannot see why the word "high" has been eliminated, when referring to persons having high judicial functions. I have a case in mind. This has to do with a gentleman who has been a county court judge in a great province. I believe, in fact, that he has headed the judges in his district, and he has now retired. That judge was an authority on criminal matters. He is in good health, and could do good work. In my opinion he should not be eliminated simply because a county court or district court judge is not. considered as one holding a high judicial position. As a matter of fact, the man I have in mind is a good deal more qualified than most of the judges of the higher courts.
There again, however, the responsibility will be ours not to appoint anybody who would not be qualified to occupy the position. It has been stated quite frequently that public opinion in Canada is strongly opposed to the defence of Canada regulations. We have had a demonstration quite recently which indicates that that is not so. A by-election was held in Edmonton East. A gentleman journeyed from Toronto to Edmonton to offer himself as a candidate opposed to the defence of Canada regulations. In his campaign he was helped by the hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mrs. Nielsen), who travelled to Edmonton to attack the regulations. The hon.
member said even that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was worse than Hitler. She said that he was a worse dictator than Hitler, because he could do anything. Well, it appears that the electors of Edmonton East believed that I could be safely trusted to do better than Hitler, so far as the matter of dictatorship is concerned, and neither Mr. MacLeod nor the hon. member for North Battleford had great success in their attack upon the defence of Canada regulations.
I should not like to close without expressing an appreciation of those whose work I am in the best position to judge. I pay tribute to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the devotion of all its members and the satisfactory results of their work. At no time have I had to make complaint either as to their ability or as to the conscientious manner in which they have acted in the execution of their duties. When this war is over-and I hope it will be before too many years, and we shall have achieved victory-I believe the people of Canada will have reason to be grateful to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for the way in which they have done their work in keeping order in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few minutes in what I have to say. When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) , who represented this group on the committee, spoke this morning, he made a clear statement of our position in the matter.
I should like to put the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) right about a remark he made which is not in accordance with the facts. He referred to the leader of this group, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre ,(Mr. Woodsworth), as having made a trip to Russia. The hon. member made that trip on his own; he was not a guest of the soviet government, and to the best of my knowledge he was not received with open arms. Therefore the insinuation or implication contained in the remark of the leader of the opposition is not relevant at this time.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton). I think he stated the case very well. We realize that the defence of Canada regulations are necessary at this time. Our complaint is in connection with the administration. We consider that the changes suggested by the committee which scrutinized these regulations will be beneficial. I have a good deal of confidence in the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). If he had complete jurisdiction, I am sure that he would see that justice was done. What I am concerned about, however, is the fact that a certain

Defence of Canada Regulations
amount of jurisdiction is delegated to the provinces. I am not so confident as to how that power will 'be used.
I represent a coal mining constituency, and I should like to refer briefly to an order in council which was passed on June 6, 1941. I think there is an ulterior motive in the passing of this order in council at this time. The Montreal Gazette of June 6 states:
Civil authorities administering the defence of Canada regulations were given far-reaching powers to prevent slowing up or unauthorized stoppage of coal mine production by an order in council adopted to-day and announced by J. McG. Stewart, coal administrator.
Further on it states:
They said the order is aimed at agitators, small groups who might create a partial stoppage of production based on trivial causes, and all illegal interference with production.
Personally I do not like the phrasing of that statement which apparently was issued1 by authority of the coal administrator. I find it hard to understand why an order in council like that should be passed on a day when this house was discussing matters pertaining to labour, a bill to change the conciliation machinery and make it more workable.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: At least it should have been announced here.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FOURTH AND FINAL REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I agree that coal should be produced, but I am wondering whether this order in council will be enforced equitably. It is stated that the Object of the order in council is to prevent the slowing down of operations or illegal strikes. I think that order in council was inspired from Nova Scotia. During the past month there have been some troubles in that section of the country. My only knowledge is the press, and consequently I cannot state specifically what the causes were, but I do know that 99 per cent of the trouble in that section of the country is due to the fact that the local management has practically no authority to settle grievances. The industry in Nova Scotia suffers from absentee management. Grievances pile up, and agreements or customs which have been established over a period of years are abrogated overnight. This causes discontent, and there is built up in the minds of the men a feeling that the legitimate agencies they have established are not workable. They get the run-around in all directions. The result is a stoppage of work or a slowing down of production. The morale of the men is broken; they have no incentive to produce 100 per cent.
I should like to know if an investigation will be held to see who is responsible for any illegal stoppage or sit-down strike before this order in council is applied. I know the industry in Nova Scotia and I know the management. There is no more unjust organi-

zation existing in Canada to-day; there is no organization that is manipulated in more slime or in as insidious a way as this corporation. I am afraid that many men will be placed in a position where they cannot defend themselves. I wish to make this statement so that the Minister of Justice will hear it. I am not content to leave any situation that might arise in the province in the hands of the provincial attorney general. The provincial political organization and the coal companies have mutual interests; they work together, and I do not say that for political reasons. Before any action is taken to place anyone in an internment camp, the reasons why such action is taken should be given. As the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has said, democracy is not an abstract principle; it is a living thing that is reflected in the lives of the people. If we are not practising it, there is not much use in our talking about it.
I should like to ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. McLarty) and the Minister of Justice if this order in council will be applied to the mining companies of British Columbia. In that province men are working only two or three days a week. Will it be applied to Alberta where mines are closed down and miners must seek relief? That is sabotage of the industry. If there is to be a shortage of coal; if there is to be a famine sufficiently serious to warrant the government in taking action under this order in council, then I think it should be applied to those industries which are not functioning. A mine closed down in River Hebert, Nova Scotia, throwing 150 men out of work. The Minister of Publio Works (Mr. Cardin) stated that there would be sufficient orders from the Canadian National Railways, the principal customer of this mine, to warrant the continuation of operations. Other mines are idle. A similar situation exists in Inverness county. If this order in council is to mean anything, it should work both ways. If it is not to be applied to those sections where mines are idle because it is not sufficiently profitable to carry on operations, it should not be applied to those sections where it is profitable to operate. Before it is applied, there should be an examination of the reasons why a stoppage has occurred, and the cause should be determined. I am prepared to state here that in 99 per cent of the cases, if an impartial examination were made, the cause would be found to be not the men but the fact that they are placed in their present position through unjust manipulation by people who are not concerned about the war or production other than what it means to them in dollars and cents.

Mr. Speaker, I want to read two short sentences from the Toronto Telegram of Saturday last, June 7, and then ask the Minister of Labour a question. I have advised the minister that I was going to ask this question and I am sure that he will be able to give me an answer which will be satisfactory.
The article in the Toronto Telegram is headed: "G.E. Strikers Hear Warning Acts Illegal. Delegates report McLarty declined assurance conciliation board action would be speeded up." The article goes on:
Canadian General Electric Company employees from Wal'd street and Lansdowne avenue plants, now on the fourth day of their "holiday", are
Gristed Wheat

going to remain on strike despite Ottawa's warning they return to work or be liable to arrest.
About 650 strikers unanimously reaffirmed their decision by a standing vote at a mass meeting held in the Polish National Hall, Queen street and Dovercourt road to-day. There are about 850 on strike.
Before asking my question I may say that over the week-end I met by chance a number of the strikers on the street, and in conversation with them it occurred to me that there should be some way of settling the strike promptly. They really want to get back to work. I did not enter into the causes of the dispute, because I am sure the labour department has that matter in hand. I would like to ask the minister what is the procedure of the department on being informed that a strike is in the offing-because the department must know beforehand that a strike is perhaps likely to take place. What action in such circumstances does the department usually take to prevent a strike?

speakeroldname: Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS

Mr. Speaker, in every case in
which the department is advised that a labour dispute has arisen or is likely to arise, a conciliation officer of the department is sent to carry on negotiations. The men are advised, if a strike is apprehended, that a strike would be illegal, and that if there are grievances which should be righted they should make application under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. In this particular instance, however, a strike was called very suddenly without any knowledge of the Department of Labour that there was any difficulty whatever. The men and women simply walked out. Immediately this happened a conciliation officer was sent to the plant. He endeavoured to conciliate and suggested that the men and women should return to work. This they refused to do, and have refused ever since, and so far as my information goes they are still out.
On Friday evening I met a delegation of the workers of the Canadian General Electric plants in Toronto, who are now engaged in an illegal strike. I advised them that they should return to work and that when they had put themselves within the law they would have the same rights as any other employees in war industries in Canada to apply for a board of conciliation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. They advised that they were holding a meeting on Saturday morning, and on Saturday afternoon I was advised that they had decided at the meeting not to return to work. I immediately wired

I have been advised that they have not returned to work and have consequently arranged to advise the law officers of the crown as to the circumstances in connection with the matter and asked them to take such action as they deem most appropriate under such circumstances for the enforcement of the law.

Objection is against ruling of quota delivery point. For instance, a farmer declares his quota delivery point, say White Star or Davis or Crutwell dependent where farm located.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal at this time with a number of points raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) in his speech on this item on Friday last.
In the first place, the hon. member has complained that he cannot get a detailed account of the board's operations from the annual report issued by the Canadian wheat board on January 11, 1941. I am astonished at this, because the report contains a complete and detailed statement of the board's operations up to July 31, 1940.
For example, the hon. member has asked what the liability is in connection with the 42 million bushels of wheat 'carried in country elevators or in transit on July 31, 1940, for the account of the board. He has already answered his own question by quoting from the annual report, exhibit A, that the liability amounted to $28,927,925. I might add that this amount has been reduced to a very small figure, as most of the 1939 wheat has been forwarded to terminal positions.
With regard to the hon. member's request for evidence that the British authorities requested that the grain exchange should remain open, I placed on Hansard in 1940, at page 2360, this evidence with regard to the previous* sale, or to the sale of 100 million bushels of wheat last year. I should like to quote now from a cable received on May 9, 1941, from the cereals import branch of the United Kingdom ministry of food, with regard to the 120 million bushels sale.

To whom? To the minister?

3682	COMMONS
Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
To the wheat board. A copy of the telegram was sent to cne through the Department of External Affairs.
Who is the representative of the cereals import branch on the Winnipeg market?

There is no representative. I have repeatedly answered a similar question by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. The ceTeala import committee have no representative in Canada. I quote from the telegram.
Cereals of course must be assured that the market remains open.
"Cereals" means the cereals import branch of the United Kingdom ministry of food.
If they are not purchasing on the Winnipeg exchange why should they require the exchange to remain open? Is it because1 they .think that that sets the price?
The cereals import committee purchase their cash wheat on the exchange through well-known Winnipeg firms of brokers.
Does the minister mean to say that they have not someone there operating for them?
I can only repeat the answer I have given before. They have not.

On the theory that all the wheat goes to the wheat board, as contemplated by the act, why does the cereals import committee not buy direct from the wheat board, because that is the underlying principle of the Wheat Board Act, that they shall handle all the cash wheat? I know the act provides that the machinery shall be kept open. That was a consideration given to opposition members in the house of that day for concurring in that principle of the bill- But that was not in war time; that was in peace time, and to-day the same condition does not exist. So far as I am concerned, I wish to know what the true legal position is. The minister stated what the operating position is.
I suggest that the hon. member allow me to continue. He is anticipating something that I intend to place on the record. I shall be glad to answer any questions when I have finished this.

The minister is replying to a statement which I made, and I think one question would be proper here. He has stated, that the British cereals import committee buy through, or give an order to buy cash grain to a member of the exchange. How does the board know, when it is on the open market, that whoever got that order is placing it for the British cereals import committee?
I am informed that they do not know.
Then the board when selling the wheat do not know where it is going?
We are getting into rather technical matters concerning the handling of wheat sales. I am informed that the cereals import committee purchases futures from the wheat board-
That is the opposite to what the minister said a minute ago.
-and buy the cash grain from the exporters.
Then the board exchanges the option, and they have not sold any wheat. That is the effect of it.
I am informed that that is not so.
That is the way it operates.
The wheat goes out of the country on the basis of the sale.
Then the board takes an option, gets the cash wheat, takes an option and sells the wheat. They have not sold any wheat.

The hon. member also referred to the price paid by the British Ministry of Food to the Canadian wheat board for the recent purchase of 120,000,000 bushels of wheat futures. He claimed that Liverpool is advertising the price and that it is also disclosed in certain publications of the dominion bureau of statistics. His claim is incorrect. The so-called "Liverpool wheat offers" published daily by Broom-hall and reprinted in the "Monthly Review of the Wheat Situation" are all based upon seaboard offers of exporters, which are in turn based upon the open market futures price at Winnipeg plus freight, 'handling and other charges from the lake head to the seaboard position. Since these prices are based upon the open market price and not upon the

Supply-Trade

Canada Grain Act
price at which the futures were sold by the Canadian wheat board' to the British Ministry of Food, they cannot and do not indicate the price of the wheat board sale.
Regarding the customs export quantities and values of wheat, which are published monthly by the dominion bureau of statistics and which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle also claims to be indicative of the wheat board's sale price to the United Kingdom, I would state that these figures are simply the declared values shown on the export entries required for wheat shipments from the exporter or shipper, and the declared values are f.o.b. port of exit from Canada. These ports include Fort William-Port Arthur for shipments in transit to overseas destinations via the United States and Montreal and other St. Lawrence ports, as well as the Canadian maritime ports. Consequently the combined average valuation of wheat shipments from all these ports of exit from Canada cannot be related back to the open market prices, upon which the wheat export sales were based in the first instance. I table herewith the guarantee given to the clearing association by the Canadian wheat board, as follows:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister and in the exercise of the powers conferred by the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, is pleased to authorize and doth hereby authorize the Minister of Finance on behalf of the government of the Dominion of Canada to guarantee due payment of all such sum or sums as may be or become payable to the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange Clearing Association, Limited, by the said Canadian wheat board in respect of its obligations as a member of such association.
His Excellency in Council on the same recommendation is further pleased to order and doth hereby order and direct that the said guarantee shall be in the following form, or one to like effect;
"In consideration of the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange Clearing Association, Limited (hereinafter called 'the association'), permitting transactions and trades in grain made by the Canadian wheat board (hereinafter called 'the member') to be cleared through the association pursuant to the association's by-laws, rules and regulations, and in consideration of the association carrying an account with the member in connection with such transactions and trades, I, the undersigned, do hereby guarantee to the association the due payment of all sums of money which are now or shall at any time hereafter be owing to the association by the said member, whether the same shall be owing upon any open line of trades carried by the association for the said member, or for any liability contracted by the association on account of the said member, or upon any cheques, bills or notes given by the said member to the association.
Dated at Ottawa, this 30th day of December, 1935."
The usual practice of the clearing association in dealing with the grain companies is to stipulate that they may carry a certain maximum quantity of futures, based upon their financial standing, without requiring the deposit of any original margins. If this quantity is exceeded, origii al margin must be deposited for the entire quantity of futures held by the company concerned. In the case of the Canadian wheat board, operating under the guarantee of the government, the clearing association waived all requirements with regard to original margins. The wheat board has no margins with the clearing association, so that when the hon. member inquires whether the guaranteed liability of the wheat 'board in the clearing association has an influence on the government's decision to keep the grain exchange open, he is completely misunderstanding the situation, since there are no margin deposits.
Then may I ask why-

May I just finish this portion. Such a guarantee could have no influence on the matter or on the government's decision with regard to the Winnipeg grain exchange.
The daily "margin deposits" referred to in the budget resolutions merely bring the valuation of the wheat board's holdings into line with the day-to-day changes in the market prices and accordingly vary from day to day. Sometimes the clearing association issues a cheque to the board, and at other times a payment to the clearing association by the board is necessary. Therefore my answer to

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
the hon. member is that since the board did not put up margins with the clearing association, and also since the clearing association is independent of the Winnipeg grain exchange, the margin requirements cannot influence the government's decision as to whether the Winnipeg grain exchange should operate or not. There is no basis whatever for the hon. member's claim that the government could be influenced by this to keep the market open.

The hon. member for Qu'Appelle also inquires with regard to the financing of the Canadian wheat board. The government guarantees advances to the Canadian wheat board by a stated amount adjustable to the board's requirements for each season. The board then borrows from the banks against warehouse receipts. The interest rate of three per 'cent is arranged for between the board and the banks, after consultation with the Department of Finance.
The stocks of wheat held by the elevator companies for the account of the board in country elevators or in transit to terminal elevators are financed by the elevator companies. The board allows them an interest rate of 44 per cent, which is the same rate that the elevator companies are required to pay the banks from whom they borrow the money. The interest rate is higher on country elevator stocks because of the cost involved in wide distribution of small sums in the country, and because of the greater risk involved where no warehouse receipts are available as collateral.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has asked for information as to what he describes as "guaranteed accounts of the brokers." There are no such accounts. The hon. member has been misinformed on this point also. The

hon. gentleman is further misinformed when he says that the regulations bring coarse grains under the operation of the board. The provision to which he refers merely gives the board power to regulate the deliveries of coarse grains if such regulation should be necessary in 1941-42 in making the most effective use of available storage. The wheat board is not empowered to buy or handle coarse grains.
I have already mentioned that the Canadian wheat board publishes a complete and detailed annual report. The report for the crop year 1939-40 was issued last January, and the report for the crop year 1940-41 will be issued early in 1942. The board is also under continuous audit, and weekly reports of the auditors are forwarded to the government from Winnipeg as required under the act. In addition to these reports, the wheat sub-committee of the cabinet is in frequent consultation with the members of the Canadian wheat board. Hon. members will appreciate the necessity for such close cooperation in these times when the task of the board is, to say the least, not a light one, and new problems are arising from day to day.
I think, therefore, in view of these facts, that such statements as those of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle do not help the situation. If he could give one specific instance or make one definite charge as to why the operations of the wheat board will not bear the light of day, I would be glad to recommend that he be given a chance to substantiate his statements. From his remarks of last Friday it seems to me that he was just making general statements, without any precise knowledge of the grain business.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle quoted a telegram dated July 18, 1940, signed by a number of the elevator companies, offering to place their elevator systems at the disposal of the government for the duration of the war, provided that the government guarantee a return of 6 per cent on their capital investment. The hon. member asks why this offer was not accepted. The offer did receive consideration by the government last July. The decision then reached was that it would be more economical for the government to continue to have the elevator companies operate their own facilities on the basis of handling contracts entered into with them.
The hon. member has referred to the difficulty which certain shippers and other grain handling interests might have in making delivery of wheat at Fort William-Port Arthur against their futures contracts, and left the

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
impression that there was something new and unusual about such a situation. It should be obvious to the hon. member that the futures trading system is patterned to prevent such a return of out-of-position wheat, rather than to cause it. A shipper should not be penalized simply because he has protected himself in the usual way by hedging his purchases of cash wheat by the sale of an equivalent amount of wheat futures, some of which may be held by the board. The hon. member knows that one purpose of such transactions in the futures market is to enable the shipper to put wheat east of Fort William into export position, and keep his position hedged by the sale of futures. If this practice were not followed, then the intention of the act and the purpose of the board would be defeated in that shippers and exporters would not move wheat into position for overseas sale.
The hon. member seems to find something reprehensible in the fact that the shippers, grain interests and millers cannot make delivery of their wheat at Fort William. If the wheat board should insist that delivery be made it would mean that they would be engineering a vast corner, which would be entirely contrary to the act and would defeat our whole purpose of encouraging shipments and full use of eastern storage facilities. In this connection another consideration arises, which the hon. member mentioned. The shippers and millers would not be able to move wheat into position for overseas shipment or for grinding in Canada unless they receive a fair carrying charge from the futures market to offset their storage and interest costs. In this way the financing of the grain is looked after while it is in transit and in process of manufacture. Nothing should be done to hinder the free movement of wheat in these times of surplus.

First of all, I will take the last point he brought up, and this is the second time he has referred to the elevator at Port Arthur rented to McCabe Bros. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar also referred to that the other evening. I remember being in Fort William some years ago and speaking to the gentleman who is in charge of our internal storage elevators. At that time he told me he was losing money in this elevator at Port Arthur on account of the fact that the grain act was changed in 1929 and that, instead of being able to mix the different grades", they

had, from then on, to keep them separate. Then, he said, "We have an export grade, and we also have a grade that we buy by. The grade that we buy by is what we call the standard grade, and the grade that we sell by is called the 75-25-seventy-five of the average run of No. 1 northern as it comes in, and 25 per cent of the standard grade, which is the lowest sample that one can get out of that grade-with the result that the export grade is much higher than the standard grade." The result is that this elevator, the government having no elevators out in the country, would get only what might be called the mistakes in grading. If a sample of wheat was graded No. 1 northern, although, to look at it, it was only No. 2, the elevator company would decide that "that is no use to us; we will ship that to the government terminal at Port Arthur." That went down all through the grades, and the result was that this elevator was getting only the lowest which could pass that grade, and when they shipped the grain out they were unable to maintain their grades, and lost money. This happened after the grain act was changed in 1929.
The result was that, during the regime of Mr. Bennett, he concluded that if the government were going to lose money by operating the elevator, they might as well rent it. Therefore they called for tenders and rented it to McCabe Bros. From 1931 or 1932 it was rented continually at the same rate. The lease expired, I believe, in 1938, before the war broke out, and the government renewed the lease. That, of course, was a piece of good fortune for McCabe Bros., because since the outbreak of the war, grain storage space has been at a premium. But what is the government to be expected to do? Is it expected to break its contract and cancel the lease just because McCabe Bros, are making money out of it? I do not believe that anyone would seriously ask the government to cancel a contract which was made in good faith before the war began, merely because the lessees are making money out of it.
When does that lease expire?

It is pretty far-fetched

One other matter which has been mentioned, and to which I wish briefly to refer, is the demand for the closing of the grain exchange. I listened to the debate the other night, and everyone who rose in his place in this chamber said that we must close the grain exchange. I am not a champion of the exchange, but I have been growing grain for the last thirty-six or thirty-seven years, and during the whole of that time I have been hearing the cry, "Close the grain exchange; they are a lot of rascals down there in Winnipeg." It has long been a favourite pastime to call for the closing of the exchange, much as one hears people talking about the "big shots," the financial interests which are supposed to have the country by the throat, and the predatory banking interests. It is always a favourite sport to talk about these things. Yet I have never heard a man give a convincing reason why the grain exchange should be closed.
Did the Turgeon commission not say that it should be closed?

Never mind the Turgeon commission. The hon. member may give me any reason he can think of when his turn comes. I can give him some reasons against closing it. I have one right in my hand. Here I have two tickets for wheat sold in May. One lot of wheat was sold to the board, from whom I got 55} cents. Here is another ticket for wheat I sold to the grain exchange, and for which I got 57J cents.
Were both sold at the same time?
It is going to take a lot of talk to make me believe that the exchange has not played a useful part.
Were both lots of wheat sold on the same date?
The sales were about a week apart.
Did the hon. member get a participation receipt from the grain exchange?

No, I did not, but I have had a lot of them, and the hon. member can have them if he will give me one-half of the difference between what I received on those two transactions. There is, in fact, 2} cents difference; if the hon. member will give me one cent a bushel, I will let him have them all. As I have said, it would take a lot of talking to persuade me that the grain exchange
has not played a useful part, and I believe that my opinion is held by every other farmer in western Canada who is dealing in or selling wheat when he obtains that advantage by trading through the grain exchange.
Another consideration which occurs to me is this. If at the present time you close down the grain exchange, what are you going to do with your coarse grains? Where are you going to sell your flax, barley and rye? Presumably you will have to appoint a board to take them over. We shall have to have some facilities to handle these coarse grains if the exchange is closed.
There is no doubt that the grain exchange has played a useful part in the past. It has kept down the spread between cash wheat delivered at Fort William, and street wheat. Without it, the man buying wheat out in the country would have to purchase it on his own gamble. What is it going to be worth when it gets to Fort William if you do not have a grain exchange to sell the wheat for you? You must have some organization of that kind so as to narrow the spread. If you do not have it, what would be the result? Well, you buy wheat to-day, and I might not be able to get it to Fort William for two months. At the end of that time the price of wheat might be down twenty cents, and I would have to take the difference in the spread between cash wheat and spot wheat down in Fort William. Anybody who has looked into the matter knows that in this connection the grain exchange has played a useful part in the past.
Not only that. If a committee such as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle wants is set up, and it calls before it some of the members of the grain exchange, I believe it will be found that the board has been using the exchange to keep down storage costs. Mr. McFarland handled the problem in that way; he dealt in futures; and these people have to deal in futures sometimes in order to reduce the cost of storage in our terminals. There is no doubt about that.
The minister said that they do not.

Well, you will find that they do deal in futures in a certain amount.

At Fort William.

That has been provided; it cost in one year, I think something like $12,000,000; in another year, $8,000,000 or $9,000,000. If it averages about $10,000,000, that means another five cents a bushel given to wheat growers in western Canada on account of the failure of the wheat crop. That is given, not to the man who has a lot of wheat, but to the man who has no wheat; it is paid on an acreage basis. That brings it to 90 cents a bushel.
We come now to the last, namely, our participating certificates. We are told that this year it will be different from last, that on August 1 we are to have a cut-off; that all the wheat we get up to that date will be considered a government responsibility and

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
put on one side, and that, from that on, all the wheat that comes in will be dealt with as this year's crop. In other words, all the money we get for wheat after August 1 will be on this 230,000,000 bushels, that is to be kept distinct and separate. If the price of 86 cents mentioned by the hon. member for *Qu'Appelle is anything like accurate-and we know that 50,000,000 bushels anyway is going to be sold at 85 cents because it is going to be sold at 70 cents plus the processing tax- and if we have another 120,000,000 bushels, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said, sold for 86 cents, our total should be 75 cents anyway.
But the fifteen cents does not go to the farmer.

It goes to the board for
the wheat.
But the farmer does not get it.
Well, it should go to the farmer.
If it does, let us know about it.

With all these things, the participating certificates should bring somewhere in the neighbourhood of five cents a bushel; and if they bring anywhere near what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said, 86 or 86J cents. Therefore we get somewhere about 95 cents. What, then, is all the cry about not getting enough for the wheat? These are all plain facts, and out government has said that this year's wheat is to be kept separate. All wheat delivered after August 1 is bo be counted as this year's crop; when we have delivered the 230,000,000 bushels, a settlement will be made with regard to whatever we get for it, and the participating certificates will be paid. That is what we are expecting will be done.
Is that what the government said?
I understand so.
I hope that is right.

That is what I understand is to be done. Hon. members will have to ask the minister for a more definite statement, but that was what was referred to by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to it also. I refer to it again as part of the price we are to get for our wheat. Therefore we should get for the 230,000,000 bushels in the neighbourhood of 95 cents a bushel. It should not foe given just to the man who happens to have wheat. We must remember that at one
time we had a bonus of five cents a bushel on wheat, and many of us went up and down the country saying this was altogether wrong, although it was following the words of the scripture that to him that hath shall be given. We condemned the government of that time for that policy; and I say it is right that this bonus or assistance should be given to those who have poor crops, damaged crops or no crops, instead of on a bushelage basis. I believe the present system is far better than the system which was followed at that time.
There may be other questions that will arise in connection with this wheat problem. For example, there is the question of setting up a selling agency to take over this wheat; perhaps that might be a good thing to do. I am not going to say, but I think it should be investigated because some of these charges for the handling of wheat are altogether too high.

The vote we are considering this evening has to do with the administration of the Canada Grain Act, which is administered by the board of grain commissioners. That act has to do with the grading, weighing, inspection and general handling of grain, and the operation of government elevators. Up to the present I have heard no complaint with respect to the administration of the Canada Grain Act; nor have I heard any complaint with regard to the way in which the wheat board, which is under the same minister, has carried out government policy. I think most of those who have followed the situation closely will agree that during the last two years, and particularly during the last year, the wheat board has done a splendid job under most difficult circumstances. In bringing down this estimate the minister has permitted a discussion of both *the Canada Grain Act under the board of grain commissioners and the operation of the Canadian wheat board. Perhaps that is all to the good, since these matters are pretty well correlated, and we can obtain information as to both the administrative and the marketing ends at the same time.
Now that the mystery surrounding the shipment of wheat from Vancouver to north China has been cleared up, perhaps we can go ahead and deal with two or three other matters, but in this connection I think it only fair and reasonable to say that so far as this transaction was concerned, the wheat board as such was quite within its rights in what it did. As a matter of fact, if the wheat board had received an offer from anyone, suggesting a price satisfactory to them, and had not acted on that offer, they could have been criticized from the opposite point of view. I contend that the destination of the wheat

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
was a matter of government policy, and not a matter about which the wheat board should be concerned. The wheat board's job is to sell wheat, and it is for the government to say whether it will prevent such wheat from being shipped to certain countries.
This estimate provides an opportunity to discuss the question of the cost of handling wheat, which is a matter giving concern to a great many farmers; and, since the government has a part in the financing of the wheat, the matter concerns the government as well. I am bound to say that there is a general feeling in the country that in comparison with the value of the product, the handling charges are too high. I am not going to make the statement that they can and must be reduced. In a recent publication issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce I saw a statement of the cost of handling grain through the elevators in the Argentine. I am not going to refer to those costs, because I do not know the services rendered by the grain companies of the Argentine compared with the services rendered by our own companies. The grain companies are under certain definite obligations with regard to guaranteeing weight and grade, and as to financial responsibility; and from the statement concerning the Argentine I do not know that the same conditions apply there.
I think it should be pointed out that it is the job of the wheat board to market wheat, and in consequence the board is obliged to provide facilities for handling that wheat. Up to the present time the board in its wisdom has decided to use existing facilities and to make agreements with the elevator companies for the handling of the grain. This practice has been followed since the wheat board has been in operation. Therefore the matter comes down to a question of the sort of deal the wheat board can make with the elevator companies. I think it is safe to assume that the board has endeavoured at all times to make the best possible deal, because it would be entirely in its own interests, in the interests of the government and in the interests of those marketing the grain, that it should do so.
In connection with the rates for handling grain there is another feature which perhaps a good many people have overlooked. The board of grain commissioners, which administers the Canada Grain Act, each year holds a public session at which the handling charges for grain are reviewed, and at which anyone interested can attend and make representations with respect to any particular costs or charges made in connection with grain. At these meetings, of course, the trade is always represented; the wheat pools are always represented, and I suppose the milling interests

and others concerned with the marketing of grain are represented as well. I happen to know that at the meeting held last year every grain company represented pressed strongly for the continuation of the prevailing rate for the storage of grain.

That was
one-thirtieth cent?

It was one-thirtieth of a cent a bushel a day. The only protest against that charge was made by members from western Canada supporting this government. We made representations against continuing the same storage charge, and the result of those representations may be noted in the fact that the charge was reduced from one-thirtieth to one-forty-fifth of a cent a day. With all due respect to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, while it is all very well, and quite proper, for him to discuss in this house the question of handling charges and so forth, I would suggest that he also has the right to make representations at the meeting called for that purpose by the board of grain commissioners.
One other feature in connection with the handling of grain is also of importance. A few moments ago I mentioned that the board was required to make agreements for the handling of grain and that no' doubt it endeavoured to make the best deal possible. Last year, when our storage problem became so acute; when we were wondering where we were going to get storage to house the grain coming on the market, the grain trade would not commit itself to the construction of any additional storage, either temporary or permanent, unless and until it received from the government some concession with regard to taxation. In view of this circumstance, surely it must be agreed that the wheat board accomplished a great deal in its agreement with the elevator companies.
Just here I might refer to the construction of elevator annexes that has been continued this year. I think it was a mistake to continue that programme. I know that certain elevator companies went out on their own behalf in an attempt to build a quantity of additional, temporary storage space throughout the country. I do not know who was responsible for putting a check on ' that procedure, but I understand it has been stopped, and I believe that was a proper procedure to follow. So far as additional space is concerned, if it has to be acquired my contention is that the assistance might much more properly be given in connection with the building of granaries on the farms, or something of that kind. I believe it is only fair to say that our farmers are deserving

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
of a good deal more credit than has been given to them for the manner in which they housed last year's huge crop of wheat. The farmers of western Canada, who ordinarily have been accustomed to delivering their grain in the early fall months of the year, must have at some time or another held in storage on their farms upward of 200,000,000 to 225,000,000 bushels of wheat, in addition to coarse grains. No one thought there was that much storage space on the farms of western Canada. It may not have been good space-I know of houses, cellars, and all sorts of structures which were filled with grain- nevertheless it was space which could be used.
Here is another interesting point. Despite our anxiety in connection with the delivery of grain, the wheat board had available storage space in country elevators to the extent of about 50,000,000 bushels, with another 40,000,000 to 50,000,000 bushels of storage space in terminal buildings where grain could have been tucked away. Therefore had it been absolutely necessary to move some grain, that space would have been available.
Another feature which has been overlooked in connection with the handling of last year's crop is the amount of grain that was actually handled. The board, from the August to November period, took delivery of
243,000.000 bushels of wheat, in addition to coarse grains. That figure was exceeded only once in the last ten years, and that was in the year before, when a larger quantity of wheat was delivered in that fall period. I believe the wheat board is deserving of credit for the manner in which it made provision for the handling of last year's wheat crop.
Just at this point, however, I should like to refer to another feature, namely the date on which farm storage payments should be made. As I read the record, payment for farm storage by the wheat board started from November 1, last. The implied understanding of the act was that the farmer should be paid a rate of storage comparable with that paid the elevator companies. If that is so, I believe we are not being quite fair to the farmer if we are not going to begin paying storage until November 1. In my opinion it should be started at least by September 1.
I should like to refer in greater detail to the marketing of last year's crop. May I say to the minister and to the wheat board that the quota system has generally been considered satisfactory. It was the only policy which could have been carried out last fall with any degree of fairness. I have been
surprised by the manner in which business men generally have looked upon this system of delivery. By and large they wish to see it continued. They believe it is a much better policy for the farmer and for their own business to have the payments on wheat spread out over the year, rather than have the lot coming in at one time.
It is true that at the beginning of the last harvest marketing period there was a good deal of apprehension as to the condition which would probably exist because of the low delivery of wheat. Let me say that I believe the policy, as it finally worked out last fall, cannot be severely criticized. Once the minister made his statement last November, that the wheat board would accept all of this year's crop during the crop year, the credit situation was entirely relieved. Any man who was credit-worthy-I shall use that expression-had little or no difficulty in securing a loan from the bank, which in turn he paid later, the storage charge being quite sufficient to pay the interest.
That relieved the situation, so far as Manitoba was concerned, and I am bound to say I have not heard any serious complaints from any area in which there was a crop. Of course where there was no crop, or a very light one, the situation was somewhat critical. The same will happen this year with respect to the 230,000,000 bushels. The government has said that it will take the wheat during the crop year. Therefore it is a gilt-edged security, and any man who wishes to borrow on his wheat may do so.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to marketing in the United States. I contend that, apart from the price factor, our policy in Canada is not greatly unlike that of the United States. We have set up an initial price. Because of the government's statement that it will take the wheat during the crop year, credit facilities with recognized lending concerns are available for those who desire or who require to borrow money to carry on their operations.
I should like to say a word respecting the grain exchange, of which mention has been made frequently. By the way, I am reminded by one of my colleagues that the amount of wheat United States farmers are able to deliver is limited, as it is in Canada. So far as the farmer or the government is concerned, I do not think it makes a particle of difference whether the grain exchange is closed or not.
What is the price the United States farmer gets? Is it not $1.24?

I do not know just what it is to-day.
