speechtext:
May I point out to
hon. members that if they wish to ask questions they should first rise in their places. It is against the rules for an hon. member to ask a question while remaining seated.

I was going to refer to the matter of the closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange. As I said earlier, I do not think it makes any difference whether it is closed or not. So far as this country is concerned, it might as well be closed. However, as pointed out by the hon. member for Wood Mountain, we would still have the problem of marketing our coarse grains, and some machinery is necessary for that purpose. Why should we concern ourselves about a matter of this kind when practically the only purchaser of wheat we have requests that the exchange remain open? It is not doing us any harm, and therefore let us forget about any talk of closing it.
I should like to refer to another matter discussed this afternoon by hon. members, namely, the policy of the government respecting the marketing of this year's crop. The government has declared that it will take only
230,000,000 bushels. I wish to endorse the suggestion made by hon. members this evening, that all earnings acquired by this wheat be credited to that 230,000,000 bushels. If the supposition of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is correct, and if the wheat has been sold to Great Britain at either a slightly or a substantially higher price than the initial payment of the board, then that money should be earmarked for this 230,000,000 bushels. Likewise the processing tax levied on wheat consumed in this country should receive similar treatment. I hope the minister will not overlook this factor, and will see that representations are made to the government at the proper time and in the proper place.
For a few moments I should like to refer to the regulations recently passed by order in council concerning the operations of the wheat board. I refer particularly to regulation No. 17 which, as I interpret it, sets out that the landlord shall be entitled to his share of the crop delivered. If a man is renting a farm, my interpretation of this regulation is that the board is under some obligation to see that the landlord gets his one-third. I think this is entirely unnecessary, and it will cause a great deal of trouble and misunderstanding. I would say to the board that they might better get rid of that regulation and let each individual look after his own affairs according to the

agreement arrived at between landlord and tenant. Regulation No. 22 deals with the description of land, and it reads:
No person shall apply or deliver any grain on his quotas from any land other than that described in his permit. Such description shall be a correct representation of the lands owned, rented or otherwise held and farmed by the producer taking the declaration, and the producer shall ascertain that no other person entitled to proceeds of the farm has taken out a permit for such lands.
That is putting too heavy a responsibility upon the individual. After all, the wheat board has a job to do, and it should be its responsibility to see that there is no duplication of certificates.
Regulation No. 28 has to do with a man shipping grain over the platform. As I understand this regulation, a man who ships a carload of grain over the platform is obliged to forward his permit with the car to the wheat board. Having sent in that permit, he cannot deliver any more grain until he gets it back. Surely there is a difficulty there that should be recognized. A man may have a large acreage and be threshing upwards of a carload of wheat a day. He could not afford to stop and wait until his permit came back after being sent into Winnipeg. I just wanted to point out these features with respect to the regulations. I think they deserve further consideration, particularly the one with respect to the landlord and tenant shares.
Some days ago an announcement was made with respect to a proposed wheat conference to be called by the United States, to which Canada would be invited. I should like to advance this thought to the government. Having regard to the particular interest of western Canada in the marketing of wheat, I think consideration should be given to having representatives of our provincial governments attend the conference. After all, those provinces are most vitally concerned, and in my judgment it would be to the government's advantage to see that they are made conversant with any undertaking that may be proceeded with in a conference of this kind.
I come now to a matter which I have discussed briefly in this house on other occasions, namely, the finding of new industrial uses for wheat and other agricultural products. A report has recently been published setting out the far-reaching accomplishments in this regard. I think the time is coming when we must face the possibility of utilizing wheat for other purposes. This report is entitled, "Industrial Utilization of Farm Products" and is published by the North-West line elevators' association. I commend a reading of it to hon. members. At this time we are

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
considering whether we shall be able to continue with the unrestricted use of gasoline. If certain of our farm products could be turned into industrial alcohol, this would relieve the other situation to a certain extent. There is a wide field of inquiry which could be carried on, not only in western Canada but throughout all Canada Ways should be found of utilizing to better advantage the product of this great industry whose future is in jeopardy on account of conditions that exist.
I do not know whose job it would be to undertake something of this kind. The minister has under his control the national research council, the board of grain commissioners and the wheat board. Any or all of these bodies should be encouraged or advised to take up this work. I suppose it will be said that the wheat board as such has a job to do in connection with the mechanics of the marketing of wheat. The board of grain commissioners is responsible for the administration of the Canada Grain Act as it affects not only the actions of the wheat board, but the grain trade as a whole. Perhaps we could load an additional responsibility upon the board of grain commissioners; perhaps we could delegate to them the job of attempting to find new markets for wheat. We should be exploring all opportunities of trade so far as it is humanly possible to do so.
In connection with the problem of wheat we have the board of grain commissioners; we have the Canadian wheat board; we have the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; we have the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and now we have the reduction programme. I think the country expects, and I feel sure our farmers expect that the services of these various organizations, all designed fundamentally for the same thing, should be utilized in the closest cooperation and collaboration. If there is any way of bringing these groups together so that they may all work toward the same end, it is most desirable that this should be done.
Finally, I come back to what I said earlier. The duty of the wheat board is to market our wheat, and we hope they will make as good an arrangement with the elevator companies and other interests for the handling of the grain as it is possible to make. We hope they will be able to get the costs of that job down to as reasonable a figure as possible.
I repeat that I think farm storage should be paid as from September 1 instead of from November 1. I repeat that the full amount realized from the sale of this year's crop should be credited to the amount of wheat that the wheat board is going to take this year. I contend that the wheat board and 14873-234
the board of grain commissioners should continue unrelenting efforts to find new markets for our wheat as well as to study new industrial uses for wheat and other farm products.

When I spoke last Friday night it was just a few minutes before eleven o'clock, and therefore my remarks were brief. I shall be brief again to-night because there has already been quite a full discussion regarding the whole question of the marketing of wheat. I should, however, like to make reference again to-night to the question of our exports of wheat and to one or two sections in order in council P.C. 3849. The hon. member for Macdonald, when he spoke just now, said that we should not criticize the wheat board with regard to the shipment of wheat to Japan. I agree. The government must take full responsibility for that action because it is a question of government policy. This morning I, along with some other hon. members, received a couple of extracts from the Calgary Herald of June 6, and in these extracts the question was asked whether or not the wheat being shipped to Japan was going to Germany. Up to the present time we have received no answer from the government that is in any way satisfactoiy. The bald fact is that at the present time we are shipping a certain amount of wheat to Japan, and according to the Ottawa Citizen, Japan is shipping 150,000 tons of food a day to Germany. Therefore I think we can take it for granted that a certain amount of this wheat shipped from Canada is undoubtedly going to Germany to-day.
In addition, we find that in March of this year the United States shipped 1,000,000 barrels of crude petroleum to Japan, and last year, 11,500,000 barrels. It also shipped to Japan 230,000,000 pounds of copper. But are we in a position to criticize the United States for that action? The United States is not at war. We are. Yet we to-day are shipping wheat, indirectly I would say, to Germany. Just so long as we continue to take action of that kind, I do not consider that we are in a sound position to ask the people to make a supreme effort in this war.
The Calgary Herald suggests that our policy to-day towards Japan is an appeasement policy. Well, we had an appeasement policy towards Germany from 1935 to 1939, and look at the mess it landed us in! In my opinion the position is nothing more or less than a form of blackmail, and the more you give in to blackmail, the more you are blackmailed. I would say that these demands upon us by Japan will increase the more we give in to



Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
them, and the more we ship, the more we shall have to ship. Eventually war. will come, and Japan will be in just that much better position to fight against us than she is to-day.
I wish to refer to order in council P.C. 3849, section 17. I referred to it on Friday night, but I will just read part of the section again:
Whenever a quota of the grain produced on any land becomes deliverable, any producer entitled to a definite share of the crop as landlord, vendor or mortgagee, shall be entitled to have delivered in his name a share of such quota proportionate to such person's said interest in the grain, and shall have equal rights of delivery accorded to producers under the act. . . .
I pointed out that under that section of the order in council the farmer can be compelled out of the first quota of five bushels to deliver a certain percentage to the mortgage company or to the landlord, as the case may be. The question was asked, whether I was not aware that the provincial government last year stepped in to safeguard the first five bushels to the farmer. But at that time this order in council had not been passed. Had it been passed, the provincial government would not have been able to take that action. Now, with this order in council in force, the provincial government will not be able to take the same action this year that it took last year, and the result will be that the farmer will be compelled1 to split up that first quota. Therefore I would suggest that if you want to leave this section in-and the hon. member for Moose Jaw pointed out why it was necessary perhaps to have a section of this kind in the order in council-we should add a subsection at the end of section 17 with words to this effect: "Notwithstanding anything contained in the preceding section the provincial governments shall have the right to determine how much, if any, of the first five bushels delivered1 by the farmer shall be delivered to parties entitled to a definite share of the crop." I think that would take care of the situation. The section would still be left in there to make sure that the farmer would deliver a certain portion of the whole quota to the mortgage company or to the landlord; and if that section were not in there, the farmer could sell his whole quota and take the whole proceeds, and then tell the mortgage company or the landlord that his wheat was in the granary. That is, I presume, the reason why that section is there.
There is a question I wish to ask the minister. He is not here at the moment, but I will put my question and his advisers sitting before him will perhaps refer it to him on his return to the chamber. I understand that the definition of 1940 wheat acreage is the

same for the sale of wheat as it is under the summer-fallow bonus plan; that is, as defined under P.C. 3231. That being the situation, I cannot quite understand the wheat board's ruling to-day. Let me explain. I had a letter from a farmer the other day to the effect that he had 245 acres under cultivation. He had fifty acres of wheat last year, and fifty acres of wheat in 1939, and he asked me how much wheat he could sow in 1941. I stated that if he had fifty acres in 1940, and fifty acres in 1939, the amount of wheat he could sell this year would be based1 on sixty-five per cent of fifty. At the same time he had written to the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Agriculture had told him to write to the wheat board. He wrote to the wheat board, and the wheat board told him that he could sell wheat from the whole fifty acres; that it would not be sixty-five per cent of the fifty. I cannot find in the order in council anything supporting that view. According to the order in council he could only sell wheat produced off sixty-five per cent of the fifty. Can the minister explain how the wheat board arrived at that decision? I am not quarrelling with it at all because, when a man has only fifty acres of wheat, I think he should be allowed to sell the fifty. I was just wondering how the board had that amount of latitude. If a farmer had seventy acres in wheat could he sell the full seventy instead of sixty-five per cent of the seventy; or if he had eighty acres in wheat, would he be able to sell wheat off the full eighty or only off sixty-five per cent of the eighty? How high can the acreage go before the sixty-five per cent is applied? Can the minister answer that question? I cannot find it answered anywhere in the order in council.

I am very sorry, Mr. Chairman, that I was called out of the chamber for a few minutes in the midst of the remarks of my hon. friend, but I think I have caught the drift of his question. I am quite sure that circular No. 200 issued by the Canadian wheat board-
What order in council is that?
It is a circular issued to the trade by the Canadian wheat board.

Does that set aside order in council P.C. 3231 which defines the 1940 wheat acreage? I understand that that is the last order in council defining wheat acreage in 1940, and it certainly does not give any latitude of that kind. I want it understood that I am not objecting to that ruling,

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
but I am wondering under what section in the regulations the board obtains these discretionary powers.

These instructions are issued under the authority of the Canadian wheat board, the regulations being determined by them under which the quota deliveries will be set. It has nothing to do with order in council P.C. 3231. They are the regulations setting out the procedure in the handling of the wheat crop of this year.

Am I to understand, then, that the 1940 wheat acreage as defined under the regulations of the Department of Agriculture is different from that as defined under the regulations of the Department of Trade and Commerce? You have two different terms, apparently, for wheat acreage, one by the Department of Agriculture and one by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

It has been suggested, Mr. Chairman, that I place on Hansard, circular No. 195 of the Canadian Wheat Board:
The Canadian wheat board to-day made the following announcement:
On April 15 the Canadian wheat board issued a statement to the effect that the dominion government had authorized the board to restrict wheat marketings in 1941-42 to a total of 230 million bushels, which means about 223 million bushels for the western provinces. Wheat producers in the western provinces will be permitted to base their deliveries of wheat in 1941-42 on 65 per cent of their 1940 wheat acreage. This restriction will also apply to certain regions of British Columbia, such as the Peace River district, Creston, Wynndel, Vanderhoof, Armstrong and Kamloops.
In connection with implementing this policy, the Canadian wheat board announces the following decisions of special interest to wheat producers throughout the western provinces.
1.	Producers who seeded no wheat in 1940.
There are some farmers in the western provinces who, for one reason or another, did not seed any wheat in 1940 and therefore did not have 1940-41 delivery permits. Such farmers who desire to seed and deliver wheat in 1941 should make application to the board at their earliest convenience. Their cases will be considered, and if warranted, delivery quotas will be arranged for 1941-42. All applications must be made to the board prior to May 31, 1941.
That date has now been extended to the end of June.
In his application the producer should give the legal description of his land and state his total farm acreage, the number of acres in coarse grains, summer-fallow, etc., and the delivery point to be used in 1941-42.
2.	Producers who seeded an abnormally small
proportion of their land to wheat in 1940.
There are some individual farmers who in 1940 had, for one reason or another, abnormally 14873-2341
small wheat acreages. In these cases the Canadian wheat board will, on application of the producers concerned, review their wheat acreage position before establishing their delivery quotas for 1941-42. In making such an application each wheat producer must show that his 1940 acreage was substantially lower than his wheat acreage in 1939, and lower than the acreage which he Usually sows to wheat. These applications for a review of 1940 wheat acreages must be in the hands of the board as soon as possible, and no applications will be received after May 31, 1941. Upon receipt of application, forms will be mailed to the producer upon which his case can be stated.
That date also has been extended to June 30.
I believe that that statement is already on Hansard.

I
do not think it is. The other statement, No. 200, is, I believe, on Hansard.

I believe it is in
Hansard of May 2.

3.	Producers who seeded an abnormally large proportion of their land to wheat in 1940.
An examination of 1940 permits issued by the Canadian wheat board shows that in most districts throughout the west, a few producers had abnormally high wheat acreages in 1940, compared with their total farm acreage. In so far as these wheat acreages are substantially higher than usual for the farms concerned, the Canadian wheat board will, in establishing 1941-42 delivery quotas for these farmers, make such adjustments in their 1940 acreage figures as will bring them into line with their usual practice and into line with their district as a whole. This means that wheat producers who unduly expanded their wheat acreage in 1940 will have their 1941-42 delivery quotas established on the basis of wheat produced on 65 per cent of their usual wheat acreage, and in arriving at the adjustment which will be made in these exceptionally large wheat acreages in 1940, the board will consider the practice of the other farms in the district, as reported to us.
As an example, a relatively few farmers in the western provinces had over 90 per cent of their total farm area in wheat in 1940. It would be obviously unfair to the great majority of wheat producers to extend delivery quotas to these few farmers based upon wheat produced on 65 per cent of 1940 acreages. In these cases delivery quotas in 1941-42 will be based upon 65 per cent of their usual wheat acreage and the average percentage of the farm land sown to wheat in 1940 in the district concerned.
The Canadian wheat board has adopted the foregoing policies in respect to the basis of 1941-42 wheat quotas in the interests of a fair distribution of quotas among wheat producers in 1941-42. The object is to adjust some of the wide variations from usual practice that occurred in 1940 wheat seeding.
What date is that?

That is April 28, 1941.

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act

These regulations do not change the case to which I referred. They state that where there is a large difference between the 1939 and 1940 acreages, a change can be made. But I cited a case where the acreages in 1940 and 1939 were approximately the same, but in both cases they were only a very small percentage of the total cultivated acreage. Under order in council P.C. 3231, as I understand it, there will be no way of allowing that man to increase his wheat acreage. I believe that was referred to by the Minister of Agriculture, who pointed out that it was not the desire to have wheat acreage increased, and that if in the past the farmer had been sowing only a small amount of wheat, it was not intended to allow him to sow a greater amount. In this case the man wrote to me and he wrote to the Minister of Agricvdture. The minister referred him to the wheat board. I interpreted the act to him, and I got a letter back from him telling me that the wheat board had interpreted it much more generously than I had.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The regulations, you mean.

The regulations, yes. I interpreted them as they are. The wheat board, apparently, introduced a new idea, an idea which I think should be there. I believe that the wheat board and the Minister of Agriculture should have the power to allow the man to increase his wheat acreage where the amount in crop in 1939 and 1940 was only a small percentage of the total cultivated acreage. There is, however, nothing in the regulations that allows for that to be done, and I am still wondering how the wheat board were able to do it.
If the hon. gentleman will give me the name of the farmer and the particulars, I shall be glad to have the wheat board go into the matter and deal with it and advise.

That is not the point.
The wheat board did give a good interpretation; they allowed the man to sow the full acreage. But what I want to know is, what is to be the policy in the future? Are farmers who in 1939 and 1940 sowed only a small percentage of their cultivated acreage to wheat to be allowed to sow the same amount, or to sow or market only 65 per cent? I would suggest that it might be a good thing to introduce an amendment so that the same amount could be sowed. Apparently the wheat board are doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No.
fMr. J. A. MacKinnon.]

In this case they are,
because I have a letter from the man saying that the wheat board told him he could sow the whole. His name is Othen of Benton Station, Alberta. He wrote to the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Agriculture referred him to the wheat board; then I got a letter back a few days later telling me I was not interpreting the act in as liberal a way as the wheat board. I am interpreting it as it is, not as I should like it to be.
What are that man's initials?

I do not know, but he is
the only Othen there.
Would the minister say that the regulations would apply always?
There are cases where the wheat board uses its discretion in the particular circumstances.

That is, they are not
bound definitely by the regulations?
No.

That is what I said the
other day. I had three orders in council, thought I was up to date, and then I found that another had been passed. Now we find that even though we have all the orders in council we are not up to date, that the board are changing the regulations, so that members of parliament cannot be in a position to go out and tell the farmers what has actually been done. It is not a pleasant thing to give an answer and then be shown a letter from the wheat board saying that you are wrong, when you know you are right. In this case I am not criticizing the wheat board for their interpretation, but I say that the regulations should be changed to give the wheat board full power to do that without going outside the regulations.

The argument which has
just taken place bears out the contention we made earlier in the session that these matters should have been placed before a committee of the house and the regulations threshed out and brought back to the house in some kind of permanent form so that they could be explained to the people. These regulations came down before the Easter recess; we had two sets of regulations; we went home for the Easter recess and were asked to explain these regulations to the farmers. We did explain them as they were at that time; we came back, and immediately on reaching here we found that a new set of regulations had been issued which changed in some respects

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
those we had before. It leaves hon. members in an awkward position and does not make a good impression in the country as to our ability here when we go home and tell our people a certain thing and a few days later find these regulations changed. A committee of the house should have been set up, composed of members from agricultural constituencies who understand these matters, and the regulations should have been thoroughly discussed before being given publicity. That would save a great deal of confusion in the country.
One of the greatest difficulties with the farmers in the west is that they do not understand what is taking place; neither the government nor the wheat board has taken the trouble to explain these matters to them.
This afternoon the hon. member for Wood Mountain propounded something which I never heard before, that it is the grain companies who were opposed to the grain exchange. I have been in western Canada for many years; I have attended the meetings of farm organizations for years, and they have been passing resolutions asking for the abolition of the grain exchange. I never heard of the grain companies passing resolutions to that effect. But if the grain exchange is necessary at this time-and the wheat board evidently believe it is or they would not be keeping it in operation-then I think the wheat board should give an explanation to the farmers of the west as to why it is necessary.
When a farmer delivers a thousand bushels of wheat to the elevator company, he is paid for it. The elevator company put it in store; they may deliver it to the wheat board in the course of a few days or, it may be, a few months. In the meantime they pay insurance on it, and when they deliver it to the wheat board they are paid for it by the wheat board plus per cent interest for the time their money has been in use. Then the wheat belongs to the wheat board. Up to that point it has not touched the grain exchange; the handling companies to-day do not use the grain exchange. I think that is correct?
That is correct.

From then on, the wheat board should give an explanation to the farmers of western Canada as to what happens to that wheat. The farmer in western Canada understands that that wheat is sold by the wheat board to the import board in the old country. It is sold in the form of futures. Then, in order to have that wheat moved to the seaboard, it is necessary for the export
companies to buy that grain from the wheat board through the grain exchange in order finally to deliver it to the importers in Great Britain.
If a full explanation were given of the exact procedure in that matter, it might clear up a great deal of difficulty in the minds of the farmers of western Canada. Until that is done, until they understand the exact procedure, they are going to be suspicious of what is taking place. I believe the government would be well advised to do that.
With regard to the marketing of coarse grains, they are to-day marketed through the grain exchange. The farmers of western Canada received last year in November and December an average of 31 cents for oats and 42 cents for barley. This spring in April and May those grains were selling at 38 cents for oats and about 53 cents for barley. On barley that is a difference of 11 cents, which is more than the carrying charges. Immediately there is suspicion in the mind of the farmer that someone is making money out of his grain, and until the wheat board come out and show the farmer exactly what is taking place, that suspicion will remain. At this time, when it is necessary in Canada to have a 100 per cent war effort and to keep people in the right frame of mind, it would be a good thing if that suspicion in the minds of western farmers could be removed. It is going to be difficult to do; a real explanation will have to be given, because the firm belief in the minds of, I think, 75 to 85 per cent of the farmers of western Canada is that the grain exchange is making money out of them.
The hon. member for Wood Mountain produced a certificate showing that the grain exchange made an extra two or three cents a bushel on certain grades, and on some grades as much as five to seven cents at this time. I can assure him, however, that even if that is so, the suspicion is still in the minds of the western farmers that the grain exchange is there at their expense, and their expense only; and if the board can justify the use of the grain exchange at this time, they should do so, and remove that suspicion.
I take particular exception to one of the regulations issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with the marketing of grain; that is section 17, which reads:
Whenever a quota of the grain produced on any land becomes deliverable, any producer entitled to a definite share of the crop as landlord, vendor or mortgagee, shall be entitled to have delivered in his name a share of such quota proportionate to such person's said interest in the grain, and shall have equal rights of delivery accorded to producers under the act, and for such purpose the permit holder shall

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
make the permit available, but the enforcement of this provision shall be the direct concern and responsibility of the interested parties themselves and no legal obligation shall devolve on the board in respect thereto.
This fall we are going to have a limited area from which we can deliver grain. Last fall we could deliver from whatever area we had in crop at the time, and even last year a great many farmers found it difficult to finance. This year they are going to be forced by this regulation to deliver one-third of the crop, in most instances, to the mortgagee or landlord. This is going to make it difficult for them to pay their expenses. Last year, and I think again this year, the provincial legislature required the farmer to pay his threshing bill, his taxes, his seed grain, and so forth; to keep enough to put in the crop next spring, and enough to provide for his family until next year. He cannot possibly do that under the terms of this order in council; and, since this has been passed under the War Measures Act, I suppose it will supersede provincial legislation. In that event, I do not know just what will be the position this fall of the average farmer in Saskatchewan, and I believe the minister should give serious consideration to withdrawing this requirement before deliveries commence. I agree that the landlord is justified in expecting a share of the crop, but I think he might very well wait at least until after the first delivery has been made, because the farmer will require all the proceeds from that delivery to meet his expenses.
I also believe we should have some regulation with regard to the price of coarse grains this fall. I quoted figures a few minutes ago to show how prices of oats and barley had increased between last fall and this spring. This year, with a larger acreage in coarse grains, the market will be even more depressed than it was last fall; and unless the government steps in and does something with regard to a minimum price for these grains, the farmer will find himself unable to market enough wheat, to pay - his operating expenses. If he markets these coarse grains, it will be on a glutted market, and he will obtain a price which in many instances will not meet the cost of harvesting and threshing. Therefore I believe the minister should give serious consideration to the establishment of a minimum price on coarse grains this fall. Certainly the price of 70 cents a bushel for wheat this year is not going to give the farmer anything on which to come and go.
The hon. member for Wood Mountain has shown that we can obtain 95 cents for our wheat this fall, I think he said, if we follow the wishes of the Minister of Agriculture. While that may be so in some exceptional

cases, I am sure that will not be generally the case in western Canada. Take a man who had 150 acres in wheat last year. This year, according to the regulations, he will be able to market wheat from only 100 acres, and from that 100 acres he will be able to market only an average of twelve bushels to the acre. That will give him 1,200 bushels which, at 50 cents a bushel, will give him a cash return of $600. If he is in a fairly good section of Saskatchewan, he can grow that 1,200 bushels of wheat on perhaps forty acres, at thirty bushels to the acre. That will leave him 110 acres for summer-fallow which, at $4 an acre, will give him a bonus of $440, making a total return of $1,040 for his wheat. That works out at 86 or 87 cents a bushel. Last year he threshed 4,500 bushels of wheat on his 150 acres, which he sold at 50 cents a bushel, giving him an income of $2,250. This year his income will be reduced1 to $1,040, and in order to obtain that sum of money he will have to summer-fallow an additional 110 acres. Therefore, when we say he is obtaining 85 cents a bushel for his wheat, we are not telling the whole story. The fact is that his expenses are going to eat up a very large part of that 85 cents. For the thirty-two years from 1908 to 1939 inclusive, the price of wheat to the western farmer has averaged 90 cents a bushel at point of delivery. We have now reduced that figure to 50 cents a bushel, which is entirely inadequate to meet his requirements.
This morning, in speaking on the defence of Canada regulations, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George told us what he said his party believed were some of the post-war aims of the country. Among those aims was the establishment of better prices for agricultural products. If that is the policy of the government, they should set an example now by giving better prices. The people will have much more confidence in what the government will do after the war if they take a step in this direction now. The government of the United States has done something along this line; and while we may not be able to go as far as they have gone, still I think we should at least make some move in that direction, in order to show the people of western Canada and the farmers of this country generally that we believe in, and are willing to act on, what we are talking about.

This item provides $104,648.50 for the administration of the Canada Grain Act. We have had some sixteen or seventeen inquiries into the production and marketing of grain, and when the grain board was appointed it was said that there would be no more politics in the administration of this great asset. We had an opportunity, both before and after the war

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
started, to do something in this matter. I suggested in the house in 1937 and 1938 that the government should establish food reservoirs and grain reservoirs in England.
I suggested that the surplus crop carryover of one or two years should be moved to England and stored there for emergency purposes. However, my suggestion was not acted upon. The result is that war is now upon us, and the wheat remains in our own country, a glut upon the world's market.
Three years ago I urged upon the government that it should confer with the then secretary of agriculture in the United States, Hon. H. A. Wallace, as to the orderly marketing of grain on this continent and adopt a war policy. While there was not an actual war at that time, it was well known that it was coming and that the grain situation in this country and the world over was in a most precarious condition.
I would point out that I supported my leader's bill in 1935 for the nationalization of grain. It is a great pity that that measure was not passed as it was drafted, and in the form in which it received first and second readings. When it returned from committee one could scarcely recognize it. One of the main necessities in the creation of the wheat board was to get rid of the middleman. He flourishes now just as ever, like the green bay tree, both on the prairies and elsewhere.
Everyone in Canada is interested in the grain trade. We are concerned with the future of that great industry, and we are interested in those people who are the dirt farmers and who have had a very hard time of it. However, it is the middleman who has caused all the trouble, and he is still doing business at his old stand. One of the things which should be done immediately is the closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange, and the elimination of dealing in futures. What is the use in dealing with futures on the grain exchange when we know nothing of the future of our country, or the war, or the outcome of it, or to whom Canada may in the end belong. The war is our first concern.
In connection with one of the votes we discussed grain for about three weeks; it is again under discussion in a new form, under this vote, and much the same ground is again being gone over. Although realizing that hon. members to my left are keenly interested in the subject, I would point out that there are other important matters. If Hitler comes, there will be no grain board. He will take the grain, and everything else, and that will be the end of this country.
What are we doing about it? The people of Canada are not yet wide awake to the grave dangers we are now facing on the Atlantic, and in other theatres of war, and more time should be given as to where we now stand.
Since November 20 of last year I have been endeavouring to have two small matters attended to, namely soldiers' insurance and railway fares. Yet this house has never given it a minute or a thought while we look for recruits. We do not seem to be able to get a minute of time to discuss those problems. Instead of a Hitler war, one would think it was a grain war in which Canada is now engaged. Certainly the government of the day has a difficult problem on its hands, and its manner of handling it has not been altogether successful. The first thing the grain board must do is to get rid of the middleman. Then they must close up the grain exchange at Winnipeg, stop all trading in futures and take over most of the elevators with huge profits. There should be an endeavour to arrange with Washington the orderly marketing of wheat, and we must find a solution of not only production but marketing.
Efforts along that line have been made in the United States. We had a chance to bring about provisions for orderly marketing with them two years ago, but I am afraid we have been too late, as has occurred so often. I cannot understand why the grain board is not alive to the situation, and how it would not be aware that grain is going to alien enemies. In May, 1940, I received a return in the house showing the amount of pig iron, scrap iron, nickel, copper and other base metals which went to Germany, Japan, Italy, and yet another potential enemy country. The amounts involved were very large, and showed we were aiding the axis powers both directly and indirectly.
Germany managed to acquire an Atlantic fleet, something which she never had before, as a result of this and of the United States Neutrality Act, with the result that the grain trade was starved for lack of shipping space. I protest against permitting grain shipments to go to Japan through China, because we know Japan will get the whole of it and China nothing, just as unoccupied France had its food stolen by Germany. Certainly drastic action is needed to prevent our grain from reaching Japan. I might, in passing, refer to an article which appeared in a great newspaper called France. This article appeared on January 8, 1941, and while I shall not read it I might point out that it describes what happened to food which was intended for unoccupied France. The article describes

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
how 262 trainloads of food intended for unoccupied France, passed right through to Berlin. The same thing happens to grain which is supposed to go to China, but which passes through to Japan. The Chinese will never see it. Why does Canada do these things while our Victory loan campaign is on?
I believe the country should take a stand on this question. Are we to have no control over shipments of grain to axis powers as we had none over our scrap iron and pig iron? The farmers on the prairies will never get any relief so long as the wheat problem is in politics. It has been in politics as long as I have known it. Since confederation, matters connected with wheat have been inquired into seventeen times by boards, and since I have been in this chamber there have been twelve such inquiries. Yet the grain grower has yet to get the best of it, or fair play.
The people of this country will wake up one day when they find out that the real debates among the people's representatives in the House of Commons are being conducted in secret with no reports. They will have something to say not only about publicity handed out by government agencies and publicity boards but about the stand taken by some of the newspapers. I know of one great newspaper which spent about $35,000 to investigate the grain industry in 1923, 1924 and 1925. The result was that they brought about some reforms in the wheat situation and the export of hard wheat, and their efforts led to the Turgeon commission.
The people in the prairie provinces have been fooled for a great many years. They have been told that the wheat growing industry was a north and south free trade industry rather than an east and west industry, one which would serve the markets of the world. The result has been that they have allowed the middleman to take much more than his share. I know the government has a difficult proposition on its hands. I must, however, point out that while the House of Commons is willing to take four weeks to discuss grain problems, an hon. member cannot get four hours to discuss the war. Is this a Hitler war or a grain war? So far as I can see, it is the former.

I cannot permit this item to pass without making a few observations. I realize that hon. members representing agricultural constituencies have occupied a good deal of the time of the committee, but, judging by our accomplishments in debate, I think we might have saved ourselves the effort. A short time ago the Minister of Finance made certain changes which cost the treasury of Canada about $10,000,000. He

made those changes without protest from any hon. members. However, although hon. members representing agricultural constituencies have time and again appealed1 to the ministers concerned to give more favourable consideration to agriculture, our appeals seem to have fallen on deaf ears.
I listened this evening to the hon. member for Wood Mountain. His observations would leave the impression that he was an excellent medical doctor, but would not convince one that he is a mathematician or that he derives . his livelihood from the sale of wheat. I rather expected he would proceed to include the indemnity he will receive this year, and then make the computation that in selling a thousand bushels of wheat, and including his $4,000 indemnity, he would be receiving $5 a bushel for his wheat. If all farmers could include other items of income we would no doubt have a different picture. The fact remains, however, that the price to the farmer is 50 cents a bushel for the average grade at the average shipping point. I suggest that it is not fair to include payments the farmer will Jcceive this year for wheat he is not going to grow, or to include in his income payments available under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That is a fund to which contributions are made by the farmer as a result of having 1 per cent deducted from his grain cheques. The price the average farmer is still receiving is 50 cents a bushel for average grades at average shipping points.
As the hon. member for Melfort pointed out, this price is quite inadequate, having consideration for the cost of living and the amount of money available in other quarters in Canada. Two years ago the question of finding more money for agriculture was one which a great many people might have been worried about; but we are now spending possibly over $4,000,000 a day on our war effort, and there is no reason under the sun why we could not spend an additional amount each day to see that those engaged in the important war effort of producing food should receive their cost of production. It was the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) who said some time ago that it was not conceivable that people should be asked to produce at a loss. If it is not conceivable that men in industry should be asked to produce at a loss, it should follow that those engaged in producing food should not be asked to produce at a loss.
This vote provides $104,000, and the first item under it is the chief commissioner, Canada Grain Act, $12,000. Then there are two commissioners at $10,000 each and four assistant commissioners at $7,500 each. I have no doubt that these men are well qualified in

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
their respective fields, but an industry which is paying to its primary producers only 50 cents a bushel has no business paying to those who are administering some phases of the industry salaries ranging from S7,500 to $12,000. If those who are responsible for formulating agricultural policy had to change places with those who produce our foodstuffs and make a living from selling wheat at 50 cents a bushel with the cost of production as high as we have it at the present time, they would soon make many radical changes in the agricultural policies of Canada. Those who are advising the minister should consider finding ways and means of seeing that the initial price to the farmer for 1941 is increased above that which is proposed.
There has been a good deal of discussion regarding the Winnipeg grain exchange, and the hon. member for Wood Mountain has said that he has heard no good reason why the exchange should be closed. I suggest that he travel through that area of Winnipeg where those who have made fortunes on the grain exchange live and compare their environment with that of those who produce wheat on the farms. He would then see a good reason why the exchange should be closed. I am not at all impressed by the answer given by the minister this year as well as last that it is the desire of our customers across the ocean that this market should be kept open. I cannot see what purpose is being served that warrants this expenditure of time and labour. I am sure that the men engaged in making a living round the Winnipeg grain exchange are well trained, and I feel sure they could make a more valuable contribution to our war effort than they are now making. The time has come when every able-bodied person in Canada should be making his maximum contribution in the field where he is most needed. The operations of the grain exchange at this particular stage do not warrant the tremendous outlay of material and capital necessary to maintain that institution.
Some mention was made by the minister of the complaint of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar about the generous relief provided for certain brokers. My understanding of what the minister said is that they were simply carrying out the terms of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. Section 8, paragraph (i) reads:
8. It shall be the duty of the board:-
(i)	in selling and disposing of wheat as by this act provided, to utilize and employ without discrimination such marketing agencies, including commission merchants, brokers, elevator men, exporters and other persons engaged in or operating facilities for the selling and handling of wheat, as the board in its discretion may determine;
(j)	to offer continuously wheat for sale in the markets of the world through the established channels: Provided that the board may, if in its opinion any existing agencies are not operating satisfactorily, take such steps as it deems expedient to establish, utilize and employ its own or other marketing agencies or channels.
The question was raised by the hon. member for Wood Mountain as to the difficulty there might be. in connection with the marketing of oats and barley and other coarse grains if the exchange should be closed. Section 14 of the act provides as follows:
The governor in council may approve of the provisions of this act being made applicable to oats, barley, rye or flax produced in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, if the board recommends that such approval be given, whereupon the provisions of this act shall mutatis mutandis apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
The machinery is already there to look after the marketing of wheat- and coarse grains in western Canada. In view of the present critical condition in agriculture the minister should not delay any longer in seeing that the suggestions made by the hon. member for Melfort and others, that -the grain exchange should be closed for the duration of the war, should foe carried out. I have here the minutes of the fifth annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Some of this material has 'been drawn to the attention of the minister before, and I urge that he consider carefully the opinions of this national organization. They recommend:
That because of the restricted deliveries and in order to maintain the income of the western farm home, steps should be taken to increase the initial payment for wheat delivered in the crop year of 1941.
I am not going to suggest the price that should be fixed, except that it be a parity price. It has been said in the committee and throughout the country that farmers can get by with fairly low prices, and 40 cents a bushel has been mentioned. On large mechanized farms where the land and equipment are free from debt it has been shown that they can operate without going into further debt, but there is one important consideration that has been lost sight of. In the past many farmers operating large holdings have been able to go into the nearby towns and cities and engage seasonal labour for a few weeks. With that seasonal labour they have been able to operate combines and tractors.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. gentleman will see how far afield he has gone from the item before the committee. The question of hiring men and operating tractors
and the price of wheat has nothing -to do with the item -under discussion. During the greater part of the evening I -have tolerated such discussion, but there has been a great deal of it



Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
which was not relevant. But the hon. member is now much beyond any latitude allowed previous speakers.
I am not the first one who has discussed the price of wheat.
I think it was arranged that hon. members should have very wide latitude under this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Was the extent of the latitude defined?
It was very broad.
I think the understanding was that the questions which have been discussed this evening should be permissible. I do not see any items in the minister's estimates that would cover them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I was not here this
afternoon. So long as the minister states that there was an agreement, I am quite satisfied.

Thank you. I appreciate your ruling.
I was pointing out that farmers who have been able to operate large holdings with up-to-date equipment have been able to take advantage of cheap labour over short periods, but those who have been available to them to operate combines and tractors over a few weeks in the summer months have gone back to the cities and towns and lived on relief for the remainder of the year. The price available to the farmer for the production of his commodity should be higher to enable those engaged in farming operations to maintain a decent livelihood during the entire year. The price proposed of 70 cents a bushel, Fort William basis, was quite inadequate in peace time, and now with rising costs of production, and with farmers and others restricted so drastically, I think the minister should give immediate consideration to increasing the price of 70 cents.
I should like to draw to his attention the recommendation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture:
That until such time as the price of wheat reaches and is maintained at a level commensurate with the price of those things that enter into the cost of producing wheat, a processing tax of not less than fifty cents a bushel be placed on all wheat milled for domestic consumption. The revenue from such tax to be added to the aggregate price received for the wheat marketed and to be available for the purpose of increasing the initial payment to the farmer.
I know some members of the house are concerned about increasing the cost of bread. Bread is a necessity of life and should be
[The Chairman.]
kept down to a low figure, but the price which the farmer gets for the wheat that enters into bread is much too low when one considers the price the baker receives. The price of bread is altogether out of line with the prices of a great many other commodities that one buys in a store. I think a 50-cent processing tax for wheat used in domestic consumption is one which the minister should consider carefully.
Here is another recommendation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture:
It is anticipated that at the end of the current crop year all existing grain storage facilities will be filled. We believe that these surpluses of bread grains may become an important factor in our war effort and that in the meantime they should be regarded as a reserve which will ensure a constant supply of wheat to Great Britain in the event of possible crop failure in the course of the war, and also be available to meet the needs of the people of Europe when the war has been won.
This objective should not be realized entirely by the farmers themselves, because it concerns the entire people of Canada that these supplies should be carried and be available when needed by Great Britain,
The next suggestion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which I should like to commend to the minister is this:
We recommend that the dominion government be asked to provide financial assistance to farmers for the construction of adequate farm storage facilities to enable the farmer to adjust his deliveries in accordance with the system outlined above.
In the United States in peace time they have given very generous assistance in providing farm storage, and what has been done in the United States in peace time should certainly be done in Canada in war time. The large payments made to elevator companies for storing the grain will amount to large sums of money during the war period, and it is only fair that the farmers should be given some of the financial assistance given to these large corporations so that the farmers can store grain on their farms. The next recommendation is:
We recommend that the dominion government authorize the Canadian wheat board to make cash advances against that portion of the 1941 wheat crop which the farmer may deliver under the arrangement outlined above during the crop year 1941-42.
Again, in this connection, might I mention that in the United States they have made advances to the farmers on some twelve commodities which are stored on the farm. With the elevator storage facilities we are going to have available in Canada this year, the government should lose no time in announcing that a cash advance will

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
be made to the farmers for the grain stored on the farm. I know there are certain difficulties in administering a scheme of this sort, but I believe it will be found that the grain handling companies in the west this fall will be very glad to cooperate with the department in arranging the details of such a scheme. It will be found that deliveries to the elevator companies will be restricted and that elevator agents will have a great deal of spare time on their hands, and I would suggest to the minister that he enlist the cooperation of all the well-known grain handling concerns with a view to having them inspect the grain on the farm, determine whether the granary facilities are suitable enough, determine the grade, and then make arrangements for an advance of at least a portion of the initial price so that the farmers will be able to get some cash to meet their taxes, store bills, and other pressing obligations which they will have to meet this fall.
The hon. member for Macdonald mentioned that farmers with good credit had little difficulty in getting advances from the banks last fall. But the situation is more serious this year, and in a great many parts of western Canada the banks have pulled up stakes because branches were losing money and have gone where there is better fishing. The result is that many farmers find themselves miles and miles away from a bank, and they are quite unknown to bankers at a distance and are unable to get any line of credit. It would be very easy for the minister and his department to make arrangements with the elevator companies to inspect the granaries, which, of course, would have to be up to standard, and have them determine the grades, and the elevator companies would assume the responsibility of seeing that the terms of the agreement were carried out because they would have an interest in the delivery of the grain. Insurance would have to be provided to make sure that the government would not lose as a result of theft or destruction of the stocks of grain by fire. At any rate I would urge that the minister give careful consideration to this last recommendation which was endorsed by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
In conclusion, I would again urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in cooperation with the Minister of Agriculture, to see that money is made available in some way or another so that those who are performing a very useful service in producing the food necessary in Canada and for Great Britain are able to get the cost of production necessary to give them a decent standard of living.

I have one or two questions I want answered by the minister. I asked a few this afternoon, and his answers did not satisfy me. We have, however, learned something to-night. We have learned that we have a critical situation, what might be termed an emergency. We have learned that the board cannot do without the grain exchange. I am just wondering what the board will do if the grain exchange decides to close of its own accord. Just what would the board do in that event? I should like to have that question answered because it is a possibility. While the hon. member for Wood Mountain was speaking, a letter delivered by air mail was put into my hands. I have it in my pocket now, and it states that the members of the exchange are definitely anxious that it should close and they would like to have a little more information with respect to the request from Britain that they should remain open. This letter states that they are under the impression that the board had asked Britain to make that request.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Who writes the letter?
That is all right. I do not have to mention that.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It does not mean much unless we know who writes it.

Much has been said this evening with respect to the regulations. I am not going to take time to go into that now, but the minister might tell us if the last one, dated May 30, is the final one. Can we tell the farmers when we go back home that that is the one under which the board is going to operate with respect to the 1941 crop?
I wish to make this statement. There is no justification for the board to pay eight cents a year, representing the present rate per bushel, on grain stored in annexes in western Canada. We know the cost of these annexes, how they are operated, and that some of them are earning over 75 per cent on their cost and will earn it again next year; and neither this board nor this government are justified at this time, when we have a war on our hands, in paying out about $25,000,000 more for storage on the grain than they should pay. By order in council they should cut the rate, if they are going to allow these operations to continue, to not more than 2i cents a bushel a year on grain stored in the annexes. That will save this country $21,000,000 and will not do an injustice to anybody.
I asked the minister certain questions. He has ignored them, and I want them answered.
I want to know, did he have any knowledge that certain Canadian exporters refused to

Supply-Trade-Canada Grain Act
have anything to do with that deal or with any deal which would probably mean that grain would be going elsewhere than to Britain-especially, to Japan?
I want to know what brokers were used in this deal.
I want to know how much of the 575,000,000 bushels is now carried in options and how much is in cash grain?
If the minister wants to answer these questions one by one as I go along, it may facilitate getting the item through. I am going to have an answer to each one of these questions. I have asked those four to start with.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, it will not. I am
going to have answers to those questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No hon. member can
say, "I want an answer." An hon. member can put a question, and if the minister does not reply to the satisfaction of the hon. member the remedy remains in his hands; he may vote the item down if he can. But no hon. member can challenge the house or the committee by saying, "I want an answer." Also, I have already drawn the attention of the committee to the rule which prohibits tedious repetitions of the same question.
Mr. MacKINNON (Edmonton West); I think the hon. member has been repeating his questions pretty much.

Not at all. They have
not been answered.

I have tried to give the answers to the best of my ability. The hon. member is now asking if I had any information regarding Canadian exporters refusing to have anything to do with a shipment of wheat which was being treated in a similar way to the wheat we have had under discussion here-for possible shipment to Japan. I have not any such information.
The hon. member asks what brokers were used. I have stated before, and repeat again, that no brokers were used in connection with that sale.
The hon. member asks how much of the supposed or the probable carryover at the end of this crop year is cash wheat and how much is under option. I am sorry I have not the information and am unable to give it at this time.
If there was another question, Mr. Chairman, I missed it.

I asked this afternoon a
question with respect to the deal which is pending with regard to changing the July into

the October future; wheat was sold for delivery on the July option and could not be delivered, owing to the facilities at Fort William being such that they could not take it. Is there a deal pending in this respect?
I am informed that it is considered inadvisable to give any further information on that point at this time.
The minister will admit that there is a deal?
No, no, not at all, Mr. Chairman.

Will the minister say
whether he is giving any consideration to changing section 17 so as to guarantee that the first quota for the farmer shall be protected?

The matter is a very difficult one, from whatever viewpoint it is regarded. I can say definitely, Mr. Chairman, that it is receiving the very serious consideration of the wheat board and the government.
I suggested an additional subsection to take care of that matter, as the minister will find reported in Hansard to-morrow.
Does the minister intend to keep the 1941 crop absolutely separate, and not mix it with the crops of 1940 and 1939?
That is a matter of government policy, to which consideration is being given.

Will the minister tell us how much storage has been paid on grain stored in annexes, also to companies which have terminal elevators rented or leased from the government, let us say, during the last six months?	-
It is obvious that, without any notice of such questions, I could not have that information available at this time.
Then, is the minister prepared to state that there will be no further regulations by order in council?

I would not undertake to state that there would be no further regulations at all. If it is found advisable, in the interests of the wheat grower of western Canada and for the sake of equity, that there should be, the government will give the matter consideration, and, it may be, bring in further regulations.

Special War Revenue Act
One other question. Will the minister consider cutting the storage rates on grain in annexes?
Does the hon. member mean, at the head of the lakes?
No; in the country annexes.

It would be very easy to say that the government will give consideration to it, but I do not propose to put it off in that way. I do not think I would care to make any comment at this time on a leading question like that.

May I ask one question directed to order in council P.C. 3849, section 27:
No permit shall be issued for a shipping point without a licensed country elevator.
One of the situations I was confronted with in this regard was that a number of farmers told me that there was no way in which they could make $25 or $30 more easily than to load a carload of their own wheat, thereby saving the elevator company's charges. Do I understand by this regulation that .that is precluded, that a farmer cannot get a permit to load over a platform unless there is an elevator at that point? In other words, if there should happen to be a siding on my farm, I cannot have a car spotted there and load my wheat if I so desire? Is that the purport and intent of that regulation?

I am informed that loading over a platform is not precluded. I want to get this question answered, hoping that the item may go through. The reason why the man is signed up to an elevator point is so that the Canadian wheat board will have a record of the yield in the district.

There is one question I want to ask regarding advances on wheat stored on the farms. It has reference to the long negotiations that took place last year between the minister and the wheat board and the elevator companies. I ask the question because the point may come up this year.
Last year the minister gave a statement to the press that the elevator companies had refused to agree to a plan for advancing loans on the security of farm-stored grain with a limited federal guarantee. What was the suggested limited federal guarantee?
I am sorry I do not place the hon. gentleman's reference.

The minister will recall the prolonged negotiations which took place. He
stayed in Ottawa a considerable time after the house adjourned in August, and negotiations went on between the elevator companies, the wheat board and the banks. Some kind of proposition was worked out; one, I think, was suggested by the provincial governments. Then he made the statement that the plan could not be worked out because the elevator companies refused to agree to the limited federal guarantee that was offered. I wish to find out how far the government and the wheat board had gone in the way of guaranteeing to the banks advances on wheat stored on the farms.

It was found on investigation that it was not necessary to give a guarantee, even limited.
Progress reported.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, June 10, 1941.
